Comparing networks across two independent groups using bgmCompare(). This example uses the ADHD dataset bundled with bgms.

title: Group Comparison
text:
Data
The ADHD dataset contains binary symptom ratings for 355 children. Column 1 is a group indicator: 1 = ADHD diagnosis (n = 146), 0 = no diagnosis (n = 209). We split on this column and analyze the first five Inattentive items in each group.

library(bgms)

data_adhd = ADHD[ADHD$group == 1, -1]
data_adhd = data_adhd[, 1:5]

data_no_adhd = ADHD[ADHD$group == 0, -1]
data_no_adhd = data_no_adhd[, 1:5]

title: Group Comparison
text:
Fit the comparison model
bgmCompare() estimates whether edge weights and category thresholds differ between the two groups.

fit = bgmCompare(x = data_adhd, y = data_no_adhd, seed = 1234)

title: Group Comparison
text:
Posterior summaries
The summary shows baseline effects and group differences. coef() provides posterior means and inclusion probabilities for both.

summary(fit)
coef(fit)

title: Group Comparison
text:
Identifying network differences
Posterior inclusion probabilities indicate how plausible it is that a given parameter differs between groups. These convert to Bayes factors in the same way as for single-group models.

title: Group Comparison
text:
Interpretation
Extract the group-specific pairwise effects and plot the network for the ADHD group.

library(qgraph)

adhd_network = matrix(0, 5, 5)
adhd_network[lower.tri(adhd_network)] = coef(fit)$pairwise_effects_groups[, 1]
adhd_network = adhd_network + t(adhd_network)
colnames(adhd_network) = colnames(data_adhd)
rownames(adhd_network) = colnames(data_adhd)

qgraph(adhd_network,
  theme = "TeamFortress",
  maximum = 1,
  fade = FALSE,
  color = c("#f0ae0e"), vsize = 10, repulsion = .9,
  label.cex = 1, label.scale = "FALSE",
  labels = colnames(data_adhd)
)

An end-to-end analysis of ordinal data using the ordinal Markov random field. This example uses the Wenchuan earthquake PTSD dataset bundled with bgms.

title: Ordinal Network
text:
Data
The Wenchuan dataset contains responses from 362 survivors of the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake on 17 posttraumatic stress items, scored on a five-point scale from “not at all” to “extremely”. We analyze a subset of the first five items.

library(bgms)
data = Wenchuan[, 1:5]
head(data)

title: Ordinal Network
text:
Fit the model
Pass the data to bgm(). Because all variables are ordinal, bgms fits an ordinal MRF with spike-and-slab edge selection by default.

fit = bgm(data, seed = 1234)

title: Ordinal Network
text:
Posterior summaries
summary() returns posterior means, standard deviations, R-hat, and effective sample sizes for all pairwise interaction and threshold parameters. coef() provides posterior means and inclusion probabilities.

summary(fit)
coef(fit)

title: Ordinal Network
text:
Edge selection
The spike-and-slab prior assigns each edge a posterior inclusion probability. Values near 1 indicate strong evidence the edge is present; values near 0 indicate strong evidence the edge is absent; values near 0.5 are inconclusive.

coef(fit)$indicator

When the prior inclusion probability equals 0.5 (the default for a Bernoulli prior), inclusion probabilities convert directly to Bayes factors:

p = coef(fit)$indicator[1, 5]
BF_10 = p / (1 - p)
BF_10

The reciprocal gives the Bayes factor in favor of exclusion:

1 / BF_10

title: Ordinal Network
text:
Interpretation
Threshold the inclusion probabilities at 0.5 to obtain the median probability network, then plot with qgraph.

library(qgraph)

median_probability_network = coef(fit)$pairwise
median_probability_network[coef(fit)$indicator < 0.5] = 0.0

qgraph(median_probability_network,
  theme = "TeamFortress",
  maximum = 1,
  fade = FALSE,
  color = c("#f0ae0e"), vsize = 10, repulsion = .9,
  label.cex = 1, label.scale = "FALSE",
  labels = colnames(data)
)

title: Ordinal Network
text:
Diagnostics
Check convergence with the R-hat and ESS columns from the pairwise summary table.

summary(fit)$pairwise

NUTS-specific diagnostics — E-BFMI, divergent transitions, tree depth, and warmup equilibration — are available via fit$nuts_diag:

fit$nuts_diag$summary
fit$nuts_diag$warmup_check

See the MCMC Diagnostics guide for interpretation of these quantities.

The bgms C++ backend is organized in five top-level directories under src/. Each directory has a distinct role, and dependencies flow downward: algorithms depend on math utilities but not on models, and the execution layer orchestrates everything.

title: C++ Architecture
text:
Design principles
Separation of concerns. Algorithms know nothing about models. A nuts_step() call receives a function logp_and_gradient(vec) → (double, vec) and returns a StepResult. The model provides the function; the algorithm does the math.
Virtual dispatch for models. All models inherit from BaseModel and override a small set of virtual methods. The chain runner calls model.logp_and_gradient() without knowing whether it is sampling a GGM or an ordinal MRF. See Model Classes.
Cloning for parallelism. Both BaseModel and BaseEdgePrior expose a clone() method that produces an independent copy. The chain runner clones the prototype once per chain before dispatching to TBB threads. See Parallel Chains.
Header-only samplers. The sampler classes in mcmc/samplers/ are header-only. They are lightweight wrappers that hold adaptation state and call algorithm functions from mcmc/algorithms/.
Rcpp interface files. The top-level .cpp files in src/ (sample_ggm.cpp, sample_omrf.cpp, sample_mixed.cpp, bgmCompare_interface.cpp) are thin Rcpp entry points. They construct C++ objects from R lists and call run_mcmc_sampler().

title: Stochastic Block Model Prior
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
The MFM-SBM (mixture of finite mixtures – stochastic block model) edge prior assigns variables to latent clusters and uses cluster-structured inclusion probabilities. Source: src/priors/sbm_edge_prior.h and sbm_edge_prior.cpp.

title: Stochastic Block Model Prior
text:
MFM-SBM formulation
The prior has three levels:

Cluster count — The number of clusters \(K\) follows a Poisson(\(\lambda\)) prior, with a mixture-of-finite-mixtures (MFM) correction that accounts for the combinatorial allocation structure.
Cluster assignments — Each variable \(i\) is assigned to cluster \(z_i \in \{1, \ldots, K\}\) with a symmetric Dirichlet prior (concentration \(\alpha_D\)) on the cluster proportions.
Block inclusion probabilities — The inclusion probability for edge \((i, j)\) depends on whether variables \(i\) and \(j\) are in the same cluster:
\[
\pi_{ij} = \begin{cases}
\pi_{\text{within}} & \text{if } z_i = z_j \\
\pi_{\text{between}} & \text{if } z_i \neq z_j
\end{cases}
\]
Within-block and between-block probabilities are drawn from Beta distributions with separate hyperparameters.

title: Stochastic Block Model Prior
text:
Gibbs updates
The update() method in StochasticBlockEdgePrior runs three sequential Gibbs steps:

1. Cluster allocations
block_allocations_mfm_sbm() updates each variable’s cluster assignment \(z_i\) by collapsed Gibbs sampling. For each variable \(i\):

Remove variable \(i\) from its current cluster
For each possible cluster \(k\) (including a new cluster), compute the conditional probability based on:

The MFM allocation prior (CRP-like with log-partition coefficients \(\log V_n\))
The likelihood of the observed edge indicators between variable \(i\) and all other variables, given the block probabilities

Sample \(z_i\) from the resulting categorical distribution

Empty clusters are removed, and the cluster labels are relabeled to be contiguous.


2. Block probabilities
block_probs_mfm_sbm() draws new within-block and between-block inclusion probabilities from their Beta full conditionals:
\[
\pi_{kl} \sim \text{Beta}\bigl(\alpha_{kl} + e_{kl},\; \beta_{kl} + m_{kl} - e_{kl}\bigr)
\]
where \(e_{kl}\) is the number of included edges between clusters \(k\) and \(l\), and \(m_{kl}\) is the total number of possible edges. The hyperparameters \(\alpha_{kl}\) and \(\beta_{kl}\) differ for within-block (\(k = l\)) and between-block (\(k \neq l\)) pairs.


3. Inclusion probability matrix
The updated block probabilities are broadcast to the full \(p \times p\) inclusion probability matrix based on the current cluster assignments.

title: Stochastic Block Model Prior
text:
Log partition coefficients
compute_Vn_mfm_sbm() precomputes the log-partition function \(\log V_n(t)\) for \(t = 1, \ldots, t_{\max}\). These coefficients encode the MFM prior on the number of occupied clusters and appear in the allocation Gibbs step. They are computed once at initialization.
The computation involves:

Poisson probabilities for the total number of components
Rising factorials (Pochhammer symbols) for the Dirichlet-multinomial allocation counts
Log-sum-exp accumulation for numerical stability

title: Group Comparison Engine
text:
Warning

How bgmCompare() works under the hood: multi-group posterior, difference parameterization, and sampler implementation. Source: src/bgmCompare/ directory.

title: Group Comparison Engine
text:
Differences from single-group bgm
The bgmCompare engine shares the same OMRF likelihood (pseudolikelihood over ordinal/Blume-Capel variables) and the same NUTS/HMC/Metropolis sampler options, but differs in three key ways:

Parameter decomposition — Group-specific parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(g)}\) are decomposed into a shared baseline \(\boldsymbol{\varphi}\) and group differences \(\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(g)}\), linked through a contrast matrix.
Separate sampler — The bgmCompare engine uses its own chain runner (run_gibbs_sampler_bgmCompare()) rather than the general run_mcmc_chain(), because the multi-group structure requires group-specific likelihood evaluations and difference selection.
Difference selection — In addition to edge selection (which edges exist in the shared graph), bgmCompare performs difference selection (which edges differ between groups).

title: Group Comparison Engine
text:
Contrast-matrix parameterization
For \(G\) groups, the per-group parameter vector \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(g)}\) is expressed as:
\[
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(g)} = \boldsymbol{\varphi} + \sum_{h=1}^{G-1} P_{gh}\, \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(h)}
\]
where \(\mathbf{P}\) is a \(G \times (G-1)\) projection (contrast) matrix. Column \(h = 0\) (the baseline \(\boldsymbol{\varphi}\)) captures the shared structure; columns \(h > 0\) (the differences \(\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(h)}\)) capture how groups deviate from the baseline.
In the flat parameter vector, the baseline and difference parameters are interleaved per effect:
[ φ_main | δ^(1)_main | ... | δ^(G-1)_main | φ_pair | δ^(1)_pair | ... ]

title: Group Comparison Engine
text:
Multi-group log-posterior and gradient
The log-pseudoposterior sums over groups. For each group \(g\):

Reconstruct group-specific parameters via the contrast matrix
Compute the pseudolikelihood using group \(g\)’s data (sufficient statistics: category counts, Blume-Capel stats, pairwise stats)
Evaluate the gradient of the pseudolikelihood with respect to the active parameters

The gradient has two components:

Observed-data gradient (gradient_observed_active()) — Projects group-level sufficient statistics into the active-parameter layout using the contrast matrix
Expected-data gradient (gradient_expected_active()) — Computes expected sufficient statistics under the current parameters using category probabilities from the variable helpers

The prior gradient adds Cauchy penalties on both baseline and difference pairwise parameters.

title: Group Comparison Engine
text:
Sampler implementation
run_gibbs_sampler_bgmCompare() orchestrates one MCMC chain. Each iteration:

NUTS/HMC/Metropolis step — Update all active parameters (baseline + differences) using the joint log-pseudoposterior
Difference selection (if active) — For each edge, decide whether the group-difference parameters are included or set to zero. Uses a spike-and-slab mechanism analogous to edge selection in the single-group model.
Main-effect difference selection (optional) — Separately select which main-effect parameters differ between groups
Edge prior update — Update inclusion probabilities (Bernoulli, Beta-Bernoulli, or SBM)
Missing data imputation (if active) — Impute missing observations per group

The warmup schedule follows the same five-stage structure as the single-group model (see Warmup Schedule).

title: Group Comparison Engine
text:
Active parameter tracking
Because difference selection can turn parameters on and off, the total_length() function recomputes the active parameter dimension at each iteration. Index maps (build_index_maps()) provide the mapping between the flat active-parameter vector and the structured (variable, group) parameter layout.
When a difference parameter is “off” (indicator = 0), it is excluded from the NUTS block. The step size and mass matrix adapt to the current active dimension.

title: NUTS Algorithm
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
The No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) is the primary MCMC algorithm used in bgms for continuous parameter sampling. It extends Hamiltonian Monte Carlo by adaptively selecting the trajectory length, eliminating the need to tune the number of leapfrog steps.
The implementation is in src/mcmc/algorithms/nuts.h and nuts.cpp, adapted from Stan’s base_nuts.hpp (BSD-3-Clause).

title: NUTS Algorithm
text:
Leapfrog integration
Each elementary step of HMC is a leapfrog integrator that approximately preserves the Hamiltonian \(H(\theta, r) = -\log p(\theta) + \frac{1}{2} r^\top M^{-1} r\):

Half-step momentum: \(r \leftarrow r + \frac{\epsilon}{2} \nabla \log p(\theta)\)
Full-step position: \(\theta \leftarrow \theta + \epsilon\, M^{-1} r\)
Half-step momentum: \(r \leftarrow r + \frac{\epsilon}{2} \nabla \log p(\theta)\)

The implementation uses a diagonal mass matrix \(M\), stored as the vector of inverse diagonal elements (inv_mass_diag).

Memoizer
The Memoizer class in leapfrog.h caches a single \((\log p, \nabla \log p)\) pair keyed by the parameter vector \(\theta\). During NUTS tree building, each leapfrog step produces a new unique \(\theta\), so the cache trivially avoids redundant evaluations at tree-node boundaries where the same \(\theta\) appears as both the end of one subtree and the start of another.

title: NUTS Algorithm
text:
Binary tree construction
NUTS builds a balanced binary tree by doubling the trajectory in a randomly chosen direction (forward or backward) at each depth level. The tree grows until one of these stopping conditions is met:

U-turn — The trajectory starts bending back. Detected by checking whether the momentum sum across the subtree is no longer moving away from the endpoints (the generalized U-turn criterion from Betancourt, 2017).
Divergence — The Hamiltonian error exceeds a threshold (default: \(\Delta H > 1000\)), indicating the integrator has entered a region of high curvature.
Maximum depth — The tree reaches max_tree_depth (default 10, corresponding to \(2^{10} = 1024\) leapfrog steps).


BuildTreeResult
Each subtree returns a BuildTreeResult struct containing:



Field
Purpose




theta_min, r_min
Leftmost (backward) endpoint


theta_plus, r_plus
Rightmost (forward) endpoint


theta_prime, r_prime
Proposed sample from this subtree


rho
Running momentum sum (for U-turn check)


n_prime
Number of valid states (for multinomial sampling)


s_prime
Continuation flag (0 = stop)


alpha, n_alpha
Acceptance probability accumulator


divergent
Whether a divergence was detected





Proposal selection
Within a valid (non-U-turning) subtree, the proposal is selected via multinomial sampling weighted by the unnormalized target density. When two subtrees are merged, the proposed sample is drawn from the combined set with probability proportional to the number of valid states in each subtree.

title: NUTS Algorithm
text:
Divergence detection
A divergence occurs when a single leapfrog step produces a Hamiltonian error \(\Delta H = H' - H_0 > 1000\). Divergences indicate that the step size is too large relative to the local curvature of the posterior. The number of divergent transitions is recorded in StepResult::NUTSDiagnostics and surfaced to the user via extract_nuts_diagnostics().

title: NUTS Algorithm
text:
Step-size heuristic
Before the first NUTS step, the heuristic_initial_step_size() function in hmc.h finds a reasonable starting step size:

Start with \(\epsilon = 1.0\)
Take one leapfrog step and compute the acceptance probability
If acceptance is above the target (0.625), double \(\epsilon\); otherwise halve it
Repeat until the acceptance probability crosses the target

This heuristic runs once at initialization and again whenever the mass matrix is updated during warmup.

title: NUTS Algorithm
text:
NUTS diagnostics
Each NUTS step records three diagnostics:

Tree depth — Number of doubling steps (0 to max_tree_depth). Consistently hitting the maximum indicates the step size may be too small.
Divergent — Whether a divergence was detected in any leapfrog step during tree building.
Energy — The Hamiltonian \(H = -\log p(\theta) + \frac{1}{2} r^\top M^{-1} r\). Used to compute E-BFMI (energy Bayesian fraction of missing information).

These diagnostics are collected per chain and accessible via extract_nuts_diagnostics() in R.

title: NUTS Algorithm
text:
References

Hoffman, M. D., & Gelman, A. (2014). The No-U-Turn Sampler: Adaptively setting path lengths in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. JMLR, 15, 1593–1623.
Betancourt, M. (2017). A conceptual introduction to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. arXiv:1701.02434.

title: Sampler Hierarchy
text:
Warning

The sampler classes in src/mcmc/samplers/ are header-only wrappers that own adaptation state and delegate to the stateless algorithm functions in src/mcmc/algorithms/. The chain runner interacts with samplers through the SamplerBase interface.

title: Sampler Hierarchy
text:
Class hierarchy
SamplerBase                       (abstract)
├── MetropolisSampler             — element-wise Metropolis-Hastings
└── GradientSamplerBase           (abstract, owns HMCAdaptationController)
    ├── HMCSampler                — fixed-length leapfrog
    └── NUTSSampler               — adaptive tree depth
The HybridNUTSSampler variant exists for the mixed MRF, combining a NUTS step for the main parameter block with a Metropolis step for the continuous precision elements.

title: Sampler Hierarchy
Sampler Hierarchy
text:
MetropolisSampler
The simplest sampler. Each call to step():

Calls model.do_one_metropolis_step(iteration), which performs a full sweep of element-wise proposals
If the model has edge selection and the warmup schedule indicates selection is active, calls model.update_edge_indicators()
Returns the current parameters as the accepted state

Proposal standard deviations are tuned during warmup via Robbins-Monro updates (see Warmup Schedule).

title: Sampler Hierarchy
text:
GradientSamplerBase
Shared base class for HMC and NUTS. It owns an HMCAdaptationController that manages:

Dual averaging for step-size adaptation
Diagonal mass matrix accumulation via Welford’s online algorithm

The step() method in GradientSamplerBase:

Calls the concrete do_gradient_step() override (HMC or NUTS)
Passes the acceptance probability to the adaptation controller
If the mass matrix was just updated (end of a warmup window), reinitializes the step size with the heuristic

After warmup, the adaptation controller freezes and returns the smoothed step size from dual averaging.

title: Sampler Hierarchy
text:
HMCSampler
Performs fixed-length leapfrog integration. The number of leapfrog steps is set at construction from config.num_leapfrogs. Each call to do_gradient_step() invokes hmc_step() from mcmc/algorithms/hmc.h.

title: Sampler Hierarchy
text:
NUTSSampler
Uses the No-U-Turn criterion to adapt trajectory length automatically. The maximum tree depth is set from config.max_tree_depth (default 10). Returns NUTS diagnostics (tree depth, divergence flag, energy) with each step. See NUTS Algorithm for the tree-building details.

title: Sampler Hierarchy
Sampler Hierarchy
text:
Step-size adaptation
The DualAveraging class implements the Nesterov dual-averaging scheme from Hoffman and Gelman (2014). During warmup, each step’s acceptance probability is fed to the dual averager, which maintains both a current step size (for exploration) and a smoothed average (used after warmup).
Key parameters:

Target acceptance — Default 0.8 for NUTS
\(\gamma\), \(t_0\), \(\kappa\) — Shrinkage and decay parameters from the NUTS paper

title: Sampler Hierarchy
text:
Mass matrix tuning
The DiagMassMatrixAccumulator collects parameter samples during warmup stage 2 using Welford’s algorithm for numerically stable variance computation. At the end of each adaptation window, the accumulated variance is extracted as the diagonal mass matrix.
The variance estimate is blended with a prior (shrunk toward 1.0) to prevent degenerate mass matrices early in warmup when few samples are available.
When the mass matrix changes, the step size is reinitialized from scratch using the heuristic, because the optimal step size depends on the mass matrix.

title: Numerical Considerations
text:
Warning

Cross-platform numerical consistency in bgms. Source: src/math/custom_explog.h, custom_explog.cpp, custom_arma_explog.h, and explog_macros.h.

title: Numerical Considerations
text:
The problem
Standard library implementations of exp() and log() differ across platforms. The GNU C Library (glibc, used on Linux), macOS libm, and MSVC’s C runtime produce slightly different results for the same input, especially near boundary values. These differences are small (last-bit-of-precision level) but compound across thousands of MCMC iterations, causing:

Different platforms to produce different posterior samples from the same seed
CRAN check failures when comparing numerical output across architectures
Occasional test failures when expected values are computed on one platform and checked on another

title: Numerical Considerations
text:
OpenLibM solution
bgms ships a copy of the __ieee754_exp() and __ieee754_log() implementations from OpenLibM (the FreeBSD/Sun math library). These are self-contained C functions that follow IEEE 754 exactly and produce identical results on all platforms.
The implementation in custom_explog.cpp (approximately 800 lines) is the original Sun/FreeBSD code, lightly adapted to compile as C++ within an R package.

title: Numerical Considerations
text:
Platform detection
The macro system in explog_macros.h controls when custom exp/log is used:
#if (defined(_WIN32) && (!defined(CUSTOM_EXP_LOG) || CUSTOM_EXP_LOG == 0)) \
  || (!defined(_WIN32) && defined(CUSTOM_EXP_LOG) && CUSTOM_EXP_LOG != 0)
  #define USE_CUSTOM_LOG 1
#endif
The logic:

Windows — Uses custom exp/log by default because MSVC’s std::exp/std::log differ from POSIX implementations and are slower
Linux/macOS — Uses the system libm by default (which is fast and POSIX-compliant). Custom exp/log can be enabled by setting CUSTOM_EXP_LOG=1

The configure and configure.win scripts set the appropriate compiler flag in Makevars.

title: Numerical Considerations
text:
Usage in C++ code
Two levels of macros are available:



Macro
Expands to (custom)
Expands to (system)




MY_EXP(x)
__ieee754_exp(x)
std::exp(x)


ARMA_MY_EXP(X)
custom_arma_exp(X)
arma::exp(X)



The ARMA_MY_EXP variant applies element-wise custom exp/log to Armadillo matrices and vectors. It wraps custom_arma_exp() and custom_arma_log() from custom_arma_explog.h, which iterate over matrix elements and call the scalar __ieee754_exp/__ieee754_log.

title: Numerical Considerations
text:
Performance
On macOS and Linux, the system exp() and log() are highly optimized (hardware-accelerated on some architectures). The custom versions are slightly slower but guarantee cross-platform reproducibility.
On Windows with MSVC, the custom implementations are often 2–5× faster than std::exp/std::log, making the custom path beneficial for both correctness and speed.

title: Numerical Considerations
text:
EXP_BOUND and overflow prevention
The variable helpers use EXP_BOUND = 709 as the threshold for safe exponentiation, derived from the IEEE 754 double-precision range:

\(\exp(709) \approx 8.2 \times 10^{307}\) — largest representable
\(\exp(710) = +\text{Inf}\)
\(\exp(-745) \approx 5 \times 10^{-324}\) — smallest positive subnormal
\(\exp(-746) = 0\)

This bound is used throughout the codebase (not just in variable helpers) to guard against overflow before calling MY_EXP().

title: Numerical Considerations
text:
R interface
The explog_interface.cpp file exposes the custom exp/log functions to R for testing purposes. This allows verification that the custom implementations match expected values in R-level unit tests.

title: GGM Internals
text:
Precision matrix parameterization
The GGM is parameterized by the \(p \times p\) precision matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) (inverse covariance). The off-diagonal elements \(\omega_{ij}\) are the negative partial correlations (up to scaling). The model maintains an upper-triangular Cholesky factor \(\mathbf{R}\) such that \(\mathbf{R}^\top \mathbf{R} = \boldsymbol{\Omega}\) throughout sampling.
For complete data, the likelihood depends on the data only through the sufficient statistic \(\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\). The GGMModel constructor accepts either raw data or precomputed sufficient statistics.

title: GGM Internals
text:
Element-wise Metropolis
The GGM does not support gradient-based samplers because the precision matrix must remain positive definite — a constraint that is difficult to enforce in a global HMC step. Instead, each off-diagonal element \(\omega_{ij}\) is updated individually:

Propose \(\omega_{ij}^* \sim \mathcal{N}(\omega_{ij}, \sigma_{ij}^2)\)
Compute the log-acceptance ratio using the Cholesky factor
Accept or reject via Metropolis-Hastings

The proposal standard deviations \(\sigma_{ij}\) are tuned during warmup by Robbins-Monro updates targeting an acceptance rate of 0.234.

title: GGM Internals
text:
Cholesky rank-1 updates
When a single element \(\omega_{ij}\) changes by \(\delta\), the precision matrix changes by a rank-1 update: \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}' = \boldsymbol{\Omega} + \delta (\mathbf{e}_i \mathbf{e}_j^\top + \mathbf{e}_j \mathbf{e}_i^\top)\). Rather than recomputing the full Cholesky decomposition in \(O(p^3)\), bgms applies a rank-1 update to \(\mathbf{R}\) in \(O(p^2)\).

Givens rotation update
For an increase in \(\omega_{ij}\) (adding a positive-semidefinite term), the Cholesky factor is updated using Givens rotations. The update satisfies \(\mathbf{R}'^{\!\top}\mathbf{R}' = \mathbf{R}^\top\mathbf{R} + \mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^\top\).


Hyperbolic rotation downdate
For a decrease (subtracting a term), a hyperbolic rotation is used: \(\mathbf{R}'^{\!\top}\mathbf{R}' = \mathbf{R}^\top\mathbf{R} - \mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^\top\). If the result would not be positive definite (detected by a negative radicand), the downdate sets a sentinel value (R(1,0) = -2.0) and the proposal is rejected.
The Cholesky update/downdate code in src/math/cholupdate.cpp is ported from Simon Wood’s mgcv package (GPL).

title: GGM Internals
text:
Edge-specific proposals
When edge selection is active, each edge \((i,j)\) has a binary indicator \(\gamma_{ij}\). The update cycle for a single edge:

Propose inclusion/exclusion — Compute the Bayes factor for including vs. excluding the edge, using the change in log-likelihood and the prior inclusion probability
If included (\(\gamma_{ij} = 1\)) — Sample \(\omega_{ij}\) from its full conditional via the Metropolis proposal
If excluded (\(\gamma_{ij} = 0\)) — Set \(\omega_{ij} = 0\)

The order of edge updates is randomized at each iteration to avoid systematic sweep artifacts.

title: GGM Internals
text:
Log-likelihood computation
The GGM log-likelihood for \(n\) observations is:
\[
\ell(\boldsymbol{\Omega}) = \frac{n}{2} \log |\boldsymbol{\Omega}| - \frac{1}{2} \text{tr}(\mathbf{S}\boldsymbol{\Omega})
\]
The log-determinant is computed from the Cholesky factor as \(\log|\boldsymbol{\Omega}| = 2\sum_i \log R_{ii}\). The trace term uses the precomputed sufficient statistic \(\mathbf{S}\).

title: GGM Internals
text:
Missing data imputation
When na_action = "impute", the GGM imputes missing values using the conditional normal distribution implied by the current precision matrix. After imputation, the sufficient statistic \(\mathbf{S}\) is recomputed for the next likelihood evaluation.

title: Parallel Chains
text:
Warning

bgms runs multiple MCMC chains in parallel using Intel TBB (Threading Building Blocks), accessed through the RcppParallel package. The implementation is in src/mcmc/execution/chain_runner.h and chain_runner.cpp.

title: Parallel Chains
text:
Design
The entry point is run_mcmc_sampler(), which takes a prototype model, a prototype edge prior, and a sampler configuration. It follows a clone-and-dispatch pattern:

Clone — Create independent copies of the model and edge prior for each chain via model.clone() and edge_prior.clone(). Each clone has its own internal state and RNG.
Seed — Each clone is seeded with config.seed + chain_id to ensure reproducibility while avoiding correlated chains.
Dispatch — All chains are dispatched to threads. Each thread runs run_mcmc_chain() with its own model, prior, and result container.
Collect — Results are gathered and returned as a vector of ChainResult objects.

title: Parallel Chains
text:
Model and prior cloning
Both BaseModel::clone() and BaseEdgePrior::clone() perform deep copies. For the model, this includes the full parameter state, Cholesky factors (GGM), residual matrices (OMRF), and all internal buffers. For the SBM edge prior, the cluster allocations and block probability matrix are cloned.
The clone methods return unique_ptr, so each chain owns its objects exclusively with no shared mutable state between threads.

title: Parallel Chains
text:
TBB thread control
Before dispatching, bgms sets the maximum parallelism via TBB’s global control:
tbb::global_control gc(
    tbb::global_control::max_allowed_parallelism,
    no_threads
);
This limits the TBB thread pool to no_threads (the cores argument in R), respecting the user’s request even when the system has more cores available.

title: Parallel Chains
Parallel Chains
text:
Sequential fallback
When no_threads = 1 or no_chains = 1, bgms skips TBB and runs chains sequentially in a simple loop. This avoids TBB overhead for single-chain runs and simplifies debugging.

title: Parallel Chains
text:
Per-chain RNG seeding
Each chain’s RNG is a SafeRNG wrapping dqrng::xoshiro256plusplus. The seed for chain \(k\) is config.seed + k, ensuring:

Reproducibility: the same seed and chain count always produce the same results
Independence: different chains explore different random number sequences

title: Parallel Chains
text:
Progress and interrupts
The ProgressManager class handles progress display and user interrupt detection across threads.

Progress bar — Updated by each chain independently. The manager aggregates progress across chains and displays a single bar (or per-chain bars, depending on progress_type).
User interrupts — Each chain checks pm.shouldExit() between iterations. If the user presses Ctrl-C, the flag is set and all chains exit their sampling loops. The partial results are still returned (with a warning) rather than discarded.
Thread safety — Progress updates and interrupt checks use a shared print_mutex to prevent garbled console output.

title: Parallel Chains
text:
ChainResult storage
Each chain writes its output into a preallocated ChainResult:








Field
Shape
Content




samples
param_dim × n_iter
Parameter samples (post-warmup)


indicator_samples
n_edges × n_iter
Edge indicators (if edge selection)


allocation_samples
n_vars × n_iter
SBM cluster allocations (if SBM prior)


treedepth_samples
n_iter
NUTS tree depth (if NUTS)


divergent_samples
n_iter
Divergence flags (if NUTS)


energy_samples
n_iter
Hamiltonian energy (if NUTS)



The ChainResult also carries error status and user interrupt flags per chain. These are checked by the R output builder to decide whether to warn or error.

        ndraws = NULL, seed = NULL, ...)







Argument
Description




object
An object of class bgms.


newdata
A matrix or data frame with n rows and p columns. Must match the variables used in fitting.


variables
Character vector of names, integer vector of column indices, or NULL (all variables).

"probabilities" (full conditional distribution) or "response" (predicted category).


method
"posterior-mean" (use posterior means) or "posterior-sample" (average over draws).

Number of posterior draws for "posterior-sample". NULL uses all draws.

Optional random seed.

title: Edge Selection
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
Bayesian edge selection determines which edges are present in the network by placing spike-and-slab priors on the pairwise interaction parameters. When edge_selection = TRUE (the default), bgm() estimates both the edge structure and the effect sizes simultaneously.

title: Edge Selection
text:
Spike-and-slab priors
For each edge \((i, j)\), an indicator variable \(\gamma_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}\) governs whether the interaction is included in the model:

When \(\gamma_{ij} = 0\) (spike), the interaction \(\sigma_{ij}\) is set to exactly zero — the edge is absent.
When \(\gamma_{ij} = 1\) (slab), the interaction receives a Cauchy prior with scale pairwise_scale — the edge is present and the effect size is estimated.

The prior probability of inclusion is controlled by the edge_prior argument. See Prior Basics for the available options (Bernoulli, Beta-Bernoulli, Stochastic-Block).

title: Edge Selection
text:
Posterior inclusion probabilities
The posterior inclusion probability for edge \((i, j)\) is the posterior mean of \(\gamma_{ij}\): the proportion of MCMC iterations in which the edge was included. It ranges from 0 to 1:

Values near 1.0: strong evidence that the edge is present
Values near 0.0: strong evidence that the edge is absent
Values near 0.5: inconclusive (neither inclusion nor exclusion is strongly supported)

These are reported by coef(fit)$indicator and in the summary() output.

title: Edge Selection
text:
Bayes factors for edges
When the prior inclusion probability is 0.5, the posterior inclusion probability can be directly transformed into a Bayes factor:
\[
\text{BF}_{10} = \frac{p(\gamma_{ij} = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})}{1 - p(\gamma_{ij} = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})}
\]
For other prior inclusion probabilities, the Bayes factor accounts for the prior odds:
\[
\text{BF}_{10} = \frac{p(\gamma_{ij} = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}) / p(\gamma_{ij} = 0 \mid \mathbf{x})}{p(\gamma_{ij} = 1) / p(\gamma_{ij} = 0)}
\]
The reciprocal \(1 / \text{BF}_{10}\) quantifies the evidence for edge absence.

title: Edge Selection
text:
Evidence categories
The following classification, based on Kass and Raftery (1995), is a common convention:



Bayes factor
Evidence




1–3
Weak


3–10
Moderate


10–100
Strong


> 100
Decisive



The same scale applies for evidence of absence using \(1 / \text{BF}_{10}\).

title: Edge Selection
text:
Median probability model
A common summary of the posterior network is the median probability model: retain all edges with posterior inclusion probability above 0.5. This corresponds to including edges for which there is more evidence for presence than absence.
network = coef(fit)$pairwise
network[coef(fit)$indicator < 0.5] = 0

title: Edge Selection
text:
Prior guidance for edge selection
The default inclusion_probability = 0.5 with a Bernoulli prior is a standard noninformative choice. Considerations for changing it:

Sparse networks: lower the inclusion probability (e.g., 0.25) to encode a prior expectation that most edges are absent.
Dense networks: raise the inclusion probability if prior knowledge suggests many edges.
Learned inclusion probability: use edge_prior = "Beta-Bernoulli" to let the data inform the overall sparsity level.
Structured sparsity: use edge_prior = "Stochastic-Block" when edges are expected to cluster (see Edge Clustering).

The pairwise_scale parameter controls the slab width. A wider slab makes it harder for the Bayes factor to favor inclusion when the true effect is small, because the prior spreads probability over a wide range. The default of 2.5 balances sensitivity to small effects against specificity.

title: The Bayesian Approach
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
bgms uses Bayesian inference to estimate graphical models. This means that all unknown quantities — interaction parameters, edge inclusion indicators, and model structure — are treated as random variables with probability distributions. The output is a posterior distribution, not a single point estimate.

title: The Bayesian Approach
text:
Prior, likelihood, posterior
Bayesian inference combines a prior distribution with the likelihood of the observed data to produce a posterior distribution. For a parameter \(\theta\) and data \(\mathbf{x}\):
\[
p(\theta \mid \mathbf{x}) \propto p(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta) \; p(\theta)
\]

The prior \(p(\theta)\) encodes assumptions about the parameter before observing data. In bgms, priors are placed on interaction parameters, main effects, and edge indicators. See Prior Basics for details.
The likelihood \(p(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta)\) measures how well the model with parameter value \(\theta\) explains the observed data.
The posterior \(p(\theta \mid \mathbf{x})\) is the updated distribution of \(\theta\) after observing the data. All inference — point estimates, intervals, hypothesis tests — comes from this posterior.

title: The Bayesian Approach
text:
Posterior summaries
bgms summarizes the posterior with several quantities:

Posterior mean: the average of the posterior distribution. Reported by coef() and in the summary() output.
Posterior standard deviation: the spread of the posterior. A small standard deviation indicates a precise estimate.
Credible intervals: ranges that contain the parameter with a given posterior probability (e.g., a 95% credible interval). Unlike frequentist confidence intervals, credible intervals have a direct probability interpretation.

title: The Bayesian Approach
text:
Bayes factors
For edge selection, bgms uses Bayes factors to quantify evidence for the presence or absence of each edge. The inclusion Bayes factor for edge \((i, j)\) is:
\[
\text{BF}_{10} = \frac{p(\gamma_{ij} = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})}{p(\gamma_{ij} = 0 \mid \mathbf{x})} \bigg/ \frac{p(\gamma_{ij} = 1)}{p(\gamma_{ij} = 0)}
\]
where \(\gamma_{ij}\) is the binary indicator for edge inclusion. When the prior inclusion probability is 0.5, this simplifies to the posterior odds:
\[
\text{BF}_{10} = \frac{p(\gamma_{ij} = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})}{1 - p(\gamma_{ij} = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})}
\]
A Bayes factor greater than 1 favors edge inclusion; less than 1 favors exclusion. The reciprocal \(1 / \text{BF}_{10}\) gives the evidence for exclusion. See Edge Selection for interpretation guidelines.

title: The Bayesian Approach
text:
How bgms uses MCMC
The posterior distributions in bgms do not have closed-form solutions. Instead, bgms draws samples from the posterior using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. The default sampler is the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS), an adaptive form of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. bgms also supports fixed-length HMC and adaptive Metropolis-Hastings.
Multiple chains run in parallel to diagnose convergence. Key diagnostics — effective sample size (ESS), R-hat, and energy diagnostics — are described in MCMC Diagnostics. The structure of the raw MCMC output is described in MCMC Output.

title: Gaussian Graphical Model
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
The Gaussian graphical model (GGM) is a Markov Random Field for continuous variables. In bgms, the GGM is fit when variable_type = "continuous".

title: Gaussian Graphical Model
text:
The model
A GGM assumes that \(p\) continuous variables follow a multivariate normal distribution:
\[
\mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})
\]
The network structure is encoded in the precision matrix \(\boldsymbol{K} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\). A zero entry \(K_{ij} = 0\) means that variables \(i\) and \(j\) are conditionally independent given all other variables — equivalently, the edge between nodes \(i\) and \(j\) is absent.

title: Gaussian Graphical Model
text:
Partial correlations
The off-diagonal entries of the standardized precision matrix are partial correlations:
\[
\rho_{ij \cdot \text{rest}} = -\frac{K_{ij}}{\sqrt{K_{ii} K_{jj}}}
\]
A positive partial correlation means that, holding all other variables constant, higher values of \(x_i\) are associated with higher values of \(x_j\). bgms reports these partial correlations as the pairwise interaction parameters.

title: Gaussian Graphical Model
text:
Fitting a GGM
To fit a GGM, pass continuous data and set variable_type:
fit = bgm(x = continuous_data, variable_type = "continuous", seed = 1234)
The summary() and coef() methods work the same as for ordinal models. The pairwise effects in the output are partial correlations, and the diagonal of the pairwise matrix contains the precision matrix diagonal.

title: Gaussian Graphical Model
text:
Edge selection
When edge_selection = TRUE (the default), bgms applies spike-and-slab priors to the off-diagonal entries of the precision matrix. Edges with posterior inclusion probability above 0.5 have more evidence for presence than absence. See Edge Selection for details.

title: Gaussian Graphical Model
text:
Missing data
For continuous data, missing values can be imputed within the MCMC sampler by setting na_action = "impute". Missing entries are resampled at each iteration from their full conditional distribution. The default behavior is na_action = "listwise", which removes rows with any missing values before fitting.

title: Group Comparison
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
The bgmCompare() function tests for differences in network structure between groups. It estimates whether pairwise interactions and category thresholds differ across groups in an ordinal Markov Random Field.

title: Group Comparison
text:
The model
For each pair of variables \((i, j)\), the group-specific interaction is decomposed as:
\[
\theta_{ij}^{(g)} = \phi_{ij} + \delta_{ij}^{(g)}
\]
where \(\phi_{ij}\) is the baseline effect (shared across groups) and \(\delta_{ij}^{(g)}\) is the group-specific difference, constrained so that the differences sum to zero across groups. The same decomposition applies to category threshold parameters.

title: Group Comparison
text:
Defining groups
Groups can be specified in two ways:
Two separate datasets — pass x (Group 1) and y (Group 2):
fit = bgmCompare(x = data_group1, y = data_group2, seed = 1234)
Group membership vector — pass a single dataset with a group indicator:
fit = bgmCompare(x = data, group_indicator = groups, seed = 1234)
The group_indicator approach supports more than two groups.

title: Group Comparison
text:
Difference selection
When difference_selection = TRUE (the default), spike-and-slab priors are placed on the difference parameters \(\delta_{ij}^{(g)}\). The posterior inclusion probability for each difference indicates how plausible it is that the groups differ on that parameter.
By default, only pairwise interaction differences are selected (main_difference_selection = FALSE). Main effect (threshold) differences are always included. This default reflects that main effects are often nuisance parameters, and their selection can interfere with pairwise selection under the Beta-Bernoulli prior.

title: Group Comparison
text:
Interpreting the output
The summary() method reports:

Baseline effects: posterior summaries for the shared parameters \(\phi_{ij}\).
Difference effects: posterior summaries for the group differences \(\delta_{ij}^{(g)}\), including inclusion probabilities and Bayes factors.

The coef() method returns:

$pairwise_effects_groups: group-specific posterior mean pairwise interactions (baseline + difference).
$main_effects_groups: group-specific posterior mean thresholds.
$indicator: posterior inclusion probabilities for differences.

title: Group Comparison
text:
Bayes factors for group differences
When difference_probability = 0.5 (the default), the Bayes factor for a group difference equals the posterior odds:
\[
\text{BF}_{10} = \frac{p(\gamma = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})}{1 - p(\gamma = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})}
\]
A large Bayes factor indicates that the groups differ on that parameter; a small one (or equivalently, a large \(1 / \text{BF}_{10}\)) indicates that they do not.

title: Group Comparison
text:
Prior guidance for group comparison

difference_scale = 1 (default): scale of the Cauchy prior for difference parameters. This is smaller than the default pairwise_scale (2.5) because group differences are typically smaller than the effects themselves.
difference_prior = "Bernoulli" (default): fixed inclusion probability for differences. "Beta-Bernoulli" lets the data inform the overall rate of group differences.
difference_probability = 0.5 (default): prior probability that any given difference is nonzero.

title: Group Comparison
text:
References
Marsman, M., Waldorp, L. J., Sekulovski, N., & Haslbeck, J. M. B. (2025). Bayes factor tests for group differences in ordinal and binary graphical models. Psychometrika, 90(5), 1809–1842.

title: Graphical Models
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
A graphical model represents relationships among a set of variables as a graph. bgms estimates a class of undirected graphical models: pairwise Markov random fields.

title: Graphical Models
text:
Nodes and edges
In a graphical model, the \(p\) variables in a dataset are represented as nodes (or vertices) of a graph. An edge between two nodes indicates a direct statistical association between the corresponding variables, after accounting for all other variables in the model.
The absence of an edge between two nodes means the two variables are conditionally independent given the remaining variables. This is the key interpretive property of Markov random fields: the graph encodes the conditional independence structure of the joint distribution.

title: Graphical Models
text:
Conditional independence
Two variables \(X_i\) and \(X_j\) are conditionally independent given the rest if \(X_i\) provides no additional information about \(X_j\) once all other variables are observed. In the graph, this corresponds to the absence of a direct edge between nodes \(i\) and \(j\).
Conditional independence is distinct from marginal independence. Two variables may be marginally correlated (both associated with a third variable) yet conditionally independent once that third variable is accounted for. The Markov random field separates direct from indirect associations.

title: Graphical Models
text:
Markov Random Fields
A Markov random field (MRF) is an undirected graphical model in which the joint distribution factorizes according to the graph structure. For \(p\) variables with observations \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_p)\), the MRF specifies:
\[
p(\mathbf{x}) \propto \exp\left(\sum_{i} \mu_i(x_i) +
\mathbf{x}^{\sf T}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\, \mathbf{x}\right)
\]
where \(\mu_i(x_i)\) are node potentials that capture the univariate properties of variable \(i\), and \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) is a symmetric pairwise interaction matrix. The off-diagonal entry \(\phi_{ij}\) is the partial association between variables \(x_i\) and \(x_j\); when \(\phi_{ij} = 0\), the two variables are conditionally independent and the corresponding edge is absent from the graph.

title: Graphical Models
text:
Model families in bgms
bgms estimates one general MRF. The variable types in the data determine the form of the node potentials \(\mu_i(x_i)\) and the interpretation of the pairwise interactions \(\phi_{ij}\):

Ordinal MRF — all variables are binary or ordinal. Node potentials are category thresholds, and partial associations are proportional to log adjacent-category odds ratios. See Ordinal MRF.
Gaussian graphical model (GGM) — all variables are continuous. The partial associations are directly related to the precision matrix (inverse covariance matrix), whose standardized off-diagonal entries are partial correlations. See GGM.
Mixed MRF — for mixed discrete and continuous variables. The interaction matrix decomposes into blocks for discrete–discrete, continuous–continuous, and cross-type associations. See Mixed MRF.

title: Graphical Models
text:
Modeling conditional independence
The conditional independence structure — which edges are present — is typically unknown. bgms treats edge inclusion as a model selection problem, testing \(\phi_{ij} = 0\) against \(\phi_{ij} \neq 0\) for each pair of variables using spike-and-slab priors. This produces posterior inclusion probabilities that quantify the evidence for each edge. See edge selection).

Network plot
To visualize the estimated network, we select the edges with posterior inclusion probabilities 0.5 or up, and plot the result using the qgraph package.

library(qgraph)

  theme = "TeamFortress",
  maximum = 1,
  fade = FALSE,
  color = c("#f0ae0e"), vsize = 10, repulsion = .9,
  label.cex = 1, label.scale = "FALSE",
  labels = colnames(Wenchuan)
)

title: Getting Started
text:
Continuous data
For continuous variables, bgms fits a Gaussian graphical model. The interface is identical; only the variable_type argument changes.
As a continuous-data example, we use the classic examination marks dataset from Mardia, Kent, and Bibby (1979), available in the ggm package.

library(ggm)
data(marks)
head(marks)


fit_ggm = bgm(marks, variable_type = "continuous", seed = 1234)
summary(fit_ggm)

The pairwise effects are partial correlations (off-diagonal entries of the standardized precision matrix). Missing values can be imputed during sampling with na_action = "impute".

title: Prior Basics
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
This chapter explains what priors are, how bgms uses them, and when the defaults should be changed. Analysis-specific prior guidance appears on the Edge Selection, Group Comparison, and Edge Clustering pages.

title: Prior Basics
text:
What is a prior?
A prior distribution encodes assumptions about a parameter before observing data. In Bayesian inference, the prior is combined with the likelihood to produce the posterior distribution. The prior matters most when data are sparse; as data accumulate, the posterior is increasingly driven by the likelihood.

title: Prior Basics
text:
Priors in bgms
bgms places priors on three types of quantities: pairwise interaction parameters, main effect parameters, and (when edge selection is active) edge inclusion indicators. Each has a distinct role.

Pairwise interaction prior
The pairwise interactions \(\sigma_{ij}\) receive a Cauchy prior (a Student-\(t\) distribution with one degree of freedom) centered at zero. The scale is controlled by pairwise_scale (default: 2.5).
The Cauchy distribution has heavy tails, allowing large effects when supported by the data, while the peak at zero provides moderate shrinkage. In models with many variables and limited data, this regularization prevents extreme estimates.
When standardize = TRUE, the prior scale is adjusted based on the range of response scores. Variables with more categories have larger score products, which typically correspond to smaller interaction effects. Without standardization, a fixed scale is relatively wide for high-category pairs and narrow for low-category pairs. The adjustment ensures equivalent relative shrinkage across all variable pairs.


Main effect prior
Main effects (category threshold parameters for ordinal models) receive a beta-prime prior with shape parameters main_alpha and main_beta (both default to 0.5). When the two shape parameters are equal, the prior is symmetric. The beta-prime distribution is defined on the positive reals and provides light regularization of the threshold parameters.


Edge inclusion prior
When edge_selection = TRUE, each edge has a binary indicator \(\gamma_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}\) governing whether the interaction is included. The prior on these indicators is controlled by edge_prior:



Prior
Parameters
Behavior




"Bernoulli"
inclusion_probability (default 0.5)
Fixed inclusion probability, same for all edges


"Beta-Bernoulli"
beta_bernoulli_alpha, beta_bernoulli_beta (both default 1)
Inclusion probability given a Beta prior, learned from data


"Stochastic-Block"
Multiple (see Clustering)
Cluster-based inclusion probabilities with separate within/between rates

title: Prior Basics
text:
Edge priors vs. parameter priors
These two types of priors serve different purposes:

Edge inclusion priors determine how likely each edge is to be present a priori. They control the sparsity of the estimated network.
Parameter priors (Cauchy for interactions, beta-prime for thresholds) control the regularization of effect sizes. They determine how much shrinkage is applied to nonzero effects.

In a spike-and-slab framework, the “spike” is the prior mass at zero (edge excluded), and the “slab” is the Cauchy prior over effect sizes (edge included). Both matter for the posterior, but they answer different questions: the inclusion prior affects whether an edge is present, while the parameter prior affects how large the estimated effect is.

title: Prior Basics
section: Default choices and when to change them
text:
Default choices and when to change them
The defaults are designed for moderate-sized networks (5–30 variables) with ordinal data and are a reasonable starting point for most analyses:

pairwise_scale = 2.5: Appropriate for standardized ordinal data. Consider increasing it if effects are expected to be large, or decreasing it for stronger shrinkage in dense networks.
inclusion_probability = 0.5: Assigns equal prior weight to edge presence and absence. This is a standard noninformative choice. Lowering it encodes a prior expectation of sparser networks.
main_alpha = 0.5, main_beta = 0.5: A weakly informative symmetric prior. Changing these is rarely necessary unless there is strong prior information about threshold magnitudes.
standardize = FALSE: Turned off by default. Set to TRUE when variables have different numbers of response categories and comparable shrinkage across pairs is desired.

title: Edge Clustering
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
The stochastic block model (SBM) prior in bgms discovers clusters of edges in the network. Nodes are assigned to latent blocks, and edge inclusion probabilities depend on whether the two endpoints belong to the same block or different blocks.

title: Edge Clustering
text:
What is edge clustering?
In many applied networks, edges are not exchangeable: some groups of variables are densely connected while connections between groups are sparse. The SBM prior captures this structure by learning block assignments from the data. Nodes within the same block share a within-cluster inclusion probability, and edges between blocks share a (typically lower) between-cluster inclusion probability.

title: Edge Clustering
text:
Setting up the SBM prior
To use the SBM prior, set edge_prior = "Stochastic-Block" in bgm():
fit = bgm(
  x = data,
  edge_prior = "Stochastic-Block",
  seed = 1234
)
The SBM prior has several hyperparameters:








Parameter
Default
Role




beta_bernoulli_alpha, beta_bernoulli_beta
1, 1
Shape parameters of the Beta prior on within-cluster inclusion probability


beta_bernoulli_alpha_between, beta_bernoulli_beta_between
1, 1
Shape parameters of the Beta prior on between-cluster inclusion probability


dirichlet_alpha
1
Concentration of the Dirichlet prior on block assignments


lambda
1
Rate of the zero-truncated Poisson prior on the number of clusters



With the defaults, the prior is symmetric (within and between clusters have the same Beta(1, 1) prior on inclusion probability) and the number of clusters is determined by the data.

title: Edge Clustering
text:
Interpreting block structure
The extract_sbm() function retrieves the SBM results:
sbm = extract_sbm(fit)
This returns:

posterior_mean_allocations: the estimated cluster assignment for each node, computed using the method of Dahl (2006).
posterior_mode_allocations: the most frequent cluster assignment across iterations.
posterior_coclustering_matrix: a symmetric matrix where entry \((i, j)\) is the proportion of iterations in which nodes \(i\) and \(j\) were assigned to the same cluster. Plotting this matrix reveals the block structure.
posterior_num_blocks: a table of posterior probabilities for each possible number of clusters.

title: Edge Clustering
text:
Prior choices for clustering

lambda controls the expected number of clusters. A small lambda favors fewer clusters; a larger lambda allows more. The zero-truncated Poisson prior ensures at least one cluster.
dirichlet_alpha controls how evenly nodes are distributed across clusters. A value of 1 gives a uniform prior over partitions. Smaller values favor uneven cluster sizes (a few large clusters and several small ones).
The within-cluster Beta parameters control how dense within-cluster connectivity is a priori. Setting beta_bernoulli_alpha > beta_bernoulli_beta favors dense within-cluster connections.
The between-cluster Beta parameters control between-cluster connectivity. Setting beta_bernoulli_beta_between > beta_bernoulli_alpha_between favors sparse between-cluster connections.

title: Edge Clustering
text:
References
Sekulovski, N., Keetelaar, S., Haslbeck, J. M. B., & Marsman, M. (2025). Bayesian variable selection in multilevel and multi-group graphical models using a stochastic block model. Manuscript submitted for publication.

title: Mixed Markov Random Field
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
The mixed MRF is a graphical model for datasets containing both discrete (binary or ordinal) and continuous variables. bgms fits a mixed MRF automatically when variable_type includes both discrete and continuous types.

title: Mixed Markov Random Field
section: When to use a mixed MRF
text:
When to use a mixed MRF
Use a mixed MRF when the dataset contains a mix of variable types — for example, ordinal symptom ratings alongside continuous physiological measurements. Rather than discretizing continuous variables or treating ordinal scores as continuous, the mixed MRF models each variable according to its measurement scale.

title: Mixed Markov Random Field
text:
The model
The mixed MRF combines the ordinal MRF (for discrete variables) and the GGM (for continuous variables) into a single joint distribution. The model includes three types of pairwise interactions:

Discrete–discrete: interactions between ordinal/binary variables, as in the ordinal MRF.
Continuous–continuous: partial correlations between continuous variables, as in the GGM (encoded in a precision-like matrix \(K_{yy}\)).
Cross-type: interactions between discrete and continuous variables, capturing how a change in an ordinal variable’s category is associated with a shift in a continuous variable’s conditional mean.

title: Mixed Markov Random Field
text:
Data requirements
Each column in the data frame must have a corresponding entry in variable_type. Allowed types are "ordinal", "blume-capel", and "continuous". A per-variable vector is required when the types differ:
# Example: first 3 variables ordinal, last 2 continuous
fit = bgm(
  x = data,
  variable_type = c("ordinal", "ordinal", "ordinal",
                     "continuous", "continuous"),
  seed = 1234
)
bgms validates that ordinal variables contain integer-valued responses and that continuous variables are numeric. Missing values are handled by na_action ("listwise" or "impute"), just as for single-type models.

title: Mixed Markov Random Field
text:
Pseudolikelihood options
For mixed MRFs, the pseudolikelihood argument controls how the discrete full conditional distributions are approximated:

"conditional" (default): conditions on the observed continuous variables when computing the discrete full conditionals. This is faster because the discrete pseudolikelihood does not depend on the continuous interaction matrix \(K_{yy}\).
"marginal": integrates out the continuous variables, so the discrete full conditionals account for indirect associations induced through the continuous block. This is more expensive per iteration but may be more appropriate when discrete-continuous coupling is strong.

title: Mixed Markov Random Field
text:
Interpreting the output
The coef() method returns a single $pairwise matrix that contains all three types of interactions. The diagonal entries correspond to the \(K_{yy}\) diagonal (for continuous variables) or are zero (for discrete variables). The off-diagonal entries are pairwise interactions regardless of variable type.
The $indicator matrix (when edge selection is active) reports posterior inclusion probabilities for all edges, including cross-type edges.

title: Mixed Markov Random Field
text:
Fitting a mixed MRF
fit = bgm(
  x = data,
  variable_type = c("ordinal", "ordinal", "continuous", "continuous"),
  seed = 1234
)
summary(fit)
coef(fit)
The workflow — fitting, summarizing, extracting coefficients, checking diagnostics — is the same as for pure ordinal or pure continuous models.

The fit object

Posterior summaries

Posterior mean matrices
The coef() method returns posterior means in matrix form:
coef(fit)$pairwise   # p x p symmetric matrix of interaction strengths
coef(fit)$indicator   # p x p symmetric matrix of inclusion probabilities
For ordinal models, coef(fit)$main returns a matrix of category threshold means (variables in rows, categories in columns). For mixed MRFs, it returns a list with $discrete and $continuous components.

title: MCMC Output
text:
Raw MCMC samples
For custom analyses, the raw posterior draws are stored in fit$raw_samples:
str(fit$raw_samples, max.level = 1)
The structure is:

$main: list of matrices (one per chain), each with rows = iterations and columns = main effect parameters.
$pairwise: list of matrices (one per chain) for pairwise interactions.
$indicator: list of matrices for edge indicators (if edge selection was active).
$allocations: list of matrices for cluster assignments (if SBM prior was used).
$nchains: number of chains.
$niter: number of post-warmup iterations per chain.
$parameter_names: named lists of parameter labels.

Each chain is stored separately, allowing per-chain diagnostics and trace plots (see MCMC Diagnostics).

title: Ordinal Markov Random Field
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
The ordinal Markov Random Field (MRF) is a graphical model for networks of binary and ordinal variables. It is the default model in bgms.

title: Ordinal Markov Random Field
text:
The model
For \(p\) ordinal variables with observations \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_p)\), the ordinal MRF specifies the joint distribution as:
\[
p(\mathbf{x}) \propto \exp\left(\sum_{i=1}^{p} \mu_{x_i}^{(i)} +
\sum_{i<j} \sigma_{ij} \, x_i \, x_j\right)
\]
where \(\mu_{x_i}^{(i)}\) are category threshold parameters for variable \(i\) (one per category above the lowest) and \(\sigma_{ij}\) is the pairwise interaction between variables \(i\) and \(j\).
A positive interaction \(\sigma_{ij} > 0\) means that higher categories of \(x_i\) tend to co-occur with higher categories of \(x_j\), conditional on all other variables. The category thresholds control the marginal distribution of each variable.

title: Ordinal Markov Random Field
text:
Regular ordinal variables
By default, bgms treats ordinal variables as “regular”: each category above the lowest receives its own threshold parameter. This imposes no constraint on the shape of the category distribution. Variables are internally recoded to consecutive integers starting at 0.
For binary variables (two categories, coded 0 and 1), the model reduces to the Ising model, a classical MRF for binary data. The single threshold parameter controls the probability of category 1 relative to category 0.

title: Ordinal Markov Random Field
text:
Blume-Capel variables
For ordinal variables with a natural baseline or reference category (e.g., a “neutral” response), the Blume-Capel parameterization models category thresholds as a quadratic function of distance from the baseline:
\[
\mu_c = \alpha \cdot (c - b) + \beta \cdot (c - b)^2
\]
where \(c\) is the category, \(b\) is the baseline category, \(\alpha\) captures the linear trend across categories, and \(\beta\) captures the preference toward or away from the baseline:

\(\beta < 0\): the model favors responses near the baseline category
\(\beta > 0\): the model favors extreme responses (far from the baseline)

Pairwise interactions between Blume-Capel variables use centered scores \((c - b)\) rather than raw category values.
To use Blume-Capel variables, set variable_type = "blume-capel" and provide the baseline_category argument:
fit = bgm(x = data, variable_type = "blume-capel",
          baseline_category = 2, seed = 1234)
The baseline_category can be a single integer (applied to all variables) or a vector of length \(p\).

title: Ordinal Markov Random Field
text:
Pseudolikelihood
The normalizing constant of the ordinal MRF is intractable for all but the smallest networks. bgms uses a pseudolikelihood approximation: the product of full conditional distributions replaces the joint distribution. This makes estimation feasible for networks with many variables while retaining consistent parameter estimates.

title: Ordinal Markov Random Field
text:
Fitting an ordinal MRF
The ordinal MRF is the default model type. For ordinal or binary data, call bgm() directly:
fit = bgm(x = data, seed = 1234)
For Blume-Capel variables specifically:
fit = bgm(x = data, variable_type = "blume-capel",
          baseline_category = 3, seed = 1234)
The output contains posterior summaries for both threshold parameters (posterior_summary_main) and pairwise interactions (posterior_summary_pairwise).

Marsman, M., van den Bergh, D., & Haslbeck, J. M. B. (2025). Bayesian analysis of the ordinal Markov random field. Psychometrika, 90(1), 146–182.

title: MCMC Diagnostics
text:
Warning



This page has not yet passed technical or readability review.
Before interpreting results from bgm() or bgmCompare(), check that the MCMC sampler has converged and that posterior estimates are reliable. This chapter covers the diagnostic tools available in bgms.

title: MCMC Diagnostics
text:
Effective sample size (ESS)
The effective sample size estimates how many independent draws the MCMC chain is equivalent to. Correlated draws reduce the effective information per sample. A larger ESS means more precise posterior estimates.
The summary() output reports n_eff for each parameter. Values of n_eff above 400 are generally sufficient for reliable posterior means and credible intervals. Lower values suggest that more iterations may be needed.

Mixture ESS for edge-selected parameters
When edge selection is active, pairwise effects are governed by spike-and-slab priors. The parameter is set to exactly zero when the edge is excluded, creating a chain that mixes between zero and nonzero values.
Two ESS measures are reported:

n_eff: the unconditional ESS, computed from the full chain (including zeros). Measures how precisely the overall posterior mean is estimated.
n_eff_mixt: the mixture ESS, which accounts for additional uncertainty from the spike-and-slab switching. When the indicator rarely switches (fewer than 5 transitions), n_eff_mixt is suppressed.

title: MCMC Diagnostics
text:
R-hat
R-hat (split R-hat) compares the between-chain and within-chain variance. Values close to 1.0 indicate that the chains have converged to the same distribution. R-hat values above 1.01 suggest that the chains have not mixed and should be run longer.
bgms reports R-hat in summary() output and through extract_rhat().

title: MCMC Diagnostics
text:
Trace plots
Visually inspecting the sampled values across iterations is a direct way to assess convergence. Chains that have converged look like random noise fluctuating around a stable mean; chains that have not converged show trends, level shifts, or poor mixing.
Raw samples are accessible through fit$raw_samples:
param_index = 1
chains = fit$raw_samples$pairwise
nchains = length(chains)
cols = c("firebrick", "steelblue", "darkgreen", "goldenrod")

plot(chains[[1]][, param_index], type = "l", col = cols[1],
  xlab = "Iteration", ylab = "Value",
  main = "Traceplot",
  ylim = range(sapply(chains, function(ch) range(ch[, param_index]))))
if(nchains > 1) {
  for(c in 2:nchains) {
    lines(chains[[c]][, param_index], col = cols[c])
  }
}

title: MCMC Diagnostics
text:
NUTS-specific diagnostics
When using update_method = "nuts" (the default), additional diagnostics are stored in fit$nuts_diag.

E-BFMI
E-BFMI (Energy Bayesian Fraction of Missing Information) measures how efficiently the sampler explores the posterior. It compares the typical size of energy changes between successive samples to the overall spread of energies. Values close to 1 indicate efficient exploration; values below 0.3 suggest the sampler may be getting stuck.
A low E-BFMI does not necessarily mean the results are wrong, but it does warrant investigation. In models with edge selection, the most common cause is that the warmup period was too short for the discrete graph structure to equilibrate. Increasing warmup often resolves this.


Divergent transitions
Divergent transitions occur when the numerical integrator encounters regions where the posterior curvature changes too rapidly for the current step size. A small number of divergences (fewer than 0.1% of samples) is generally acceptable. Many divergences indicate that the sampler may be missing important parts of the posterior.
If divergences are frequent, increase target_accept (which reduces the step size). If that does not help, try update_method = "adaptive-metropolis" and compare results.


Tree depth
NUTS builds trajectories by repeatedly doubling their length until a U-turn criterion is satisfied. If the trajectory frequently reaches the maximum allowed depth (nuts_max_depth, default 10), the sampler may benefit from longer trajectories. Hitting the maximum depth occasionally is normal; hitting it on most iterations may indicate challenging posterior geometry. Consider increasing nuts_max_depth.

title: MCMC Diagnostics
text:
Warmup equilibration check
In models with edge selection, the discrete graph structure may take longer to reach stationarity than the continuous parameters. Even after warmup completes, the first portion of the sampling phase may still show transient behavior.
The fit$nuts_diag$warmup_check component provides diagnostics comparing the first and second halves of the post-warmup samples:







Field
Meaning




warmup_incomplete
TRUE if any indicator below suggests non-stationarity


energy_slope
Slope of energy vs. iteration; near zero = stable


slope_significant
TRUE if energy slope is significant (p < 0.01)


ebfmi_first_half
E-BFMI for the first half of post-warmup samples


ebfmi_second_half
E-BFMI for the second half


var_ratio
Ratio of energy variance (first half / second half); > 2 suggests settling



If these diagnostics suggest the chain was still settling, increase warmup and refit. If diagnostics remain problematic after doubling or tripling warmup, try refitting with update_method = "adaptive-metropolis" and compare posterior summaries. If the two samplers produce similar results, the estimates are likely trustworthy despite the warnings; if they differ, further investigation is warranted.

title: MCMC Diagnostics
text:
Recommended workflow

Inspect summary(): check R-hat (< 1.01) and ESS (> 400) for all parameters.
Check NUTS diagnostics: fit$nuts_diag$summary for divergences, tree depth saturation, and E-BFMI.
Check warmup: fit$nuts_diag$warmup_check for signs of incomplete equilibration.
Plot traces: visually inspect a few key parameters for mixing and stationarity.
If problems are found: increase warmup and/or iter, adjust target_accept, or switch samplers.
