title: bgm()
text:
Description
The bgm function estimates the pseudoposterior distribution of the parameters of a Markov Random Field (MRF) for binary, ordinal, continuous, or mixed (discrete and continuous) variables. Depending on the variable types, the model is an ordinal MRF, a Gaussian graphical model (GGM), or a mixed MRF. Optionally, it performs Bayesian edge selection using spike-and-slab priors to infer the network structure.

title: bgm()
text:
Usage
bgm(
  x,
  variable_type = "ordinal",
  baseline_category,
  iter = 1000,
  warmup = 1000,
  pairwise_scale = 2.5,
  main_alpha = 0.5,
  main_beta = 0.5,
  edge_selection = TRUE,
  edge_prior = c("Bernoulli", "Beta-Bernoulli", "Stochastic-Block"),
  inclusion_probability = 0.5,
  beta_bernoulli_alpha = 1,
  beta_bernoulli_beta = 1,
  beta_bernoulli_alpha_between = 1,
  beta_bernoulli_beta_between = 1,
  dirichlet_alpha = 1,
  lambda = 1,
  na_action = c("listwise", "impute"),
  update_method = c("nuts", "adaptive-metropolis", "hamiltonian-mc"),
  target_accept,
  hmc_num_leapfrogs = 100,
  nuts_max_depth = 10,
  learn_mass_matrix = TRUE,
  chains = 4,
  cores = parallel::detectCores(),
  display_progress = c("per-chain", "total", "none"),
  seed = NULL,
  standardize = FALSE,
  pseudolikelihood = c("conditional", "marginal"),
  verbose = getOption("bgms.verbose", TRUE)
)

title: bgm()
text:
Arguments

Data







Argument
Description




x
A data frame or matrix with n rows and p columns containing binary and ordinal responses. Variables are automatically recoded to non-negative integers (0, 1, ..., m). For regular ordinal variables, unobserved categories are collapsed; for Blume–Capel variables, all categories are retained.


variable_type
Character or character vector specifying the type of each variable. Allowed values: "ordinal", "blume-capel", or "continuous". A single string applies to all variables. A per-variable vector that mixes discrete ("ordinal" / "blume-capel") and "continuous" types fits a mixed MRF. Binary variables are automatically treated as "ordinal". Default: "ordinal".


baseline_category
Integer or vector. Baseline category for Blume–Capel variables. Can be a single integer (applied to all) or a vector of length p. Required if at least one variable is of type "blume-capel".


na_action
How to handle missing data: "listwise" (drop rows with missing values) or "impute" (single imputation during sampling). Default: "listwise".





Prior specification







Argument
Description




pairwise_scale
Scale of the Cauchy prior for pairwise interaction parameters. Default: 2.5.


main_alpha, main_beta
Shape parameters of the beta-prime prior for threshold parameters. Must be positive. Defaults: 0.5.


edge_selection
Logical. Whether to perform Bayesian edge selection. If FALSE, the model estimates all edges. Default: TRUE.


edge_prior
Prior for edge inclusion: "Bernoulli", "Beta-Bernoulli", or "Stochastic-Block". Default: "Bernoulli".


inclusion_probability
Prior inclusion probability of each edge (Bernoulli prior). Default: 0.5.


beta_bernoulli_alpha, beta_bernoulli_beta
Shape parameters for the beta distribution in the Beta–Bernoulli and Stochastic-Block priors. For the Stochastic-Block prior these are the within-cluster parameters. Defaults: 1.


beta_bernoulli_alpha_between, beta_bernoulli_beta_between
Shape parameters for between-cluster edge inclusion probabilities in the Stochastic-Block prior. Defaults: 1.


dirichlet_alpha
Concentration parameter of the Dirichlet prior on block assignments (Stochastic Block model). Default: 1.


lambda
Rate of the zero-truncated Poisson prior on the number of clusters (Stochastic Block model). Default: 1.


standardize
Logical. If TRUE, the Cauchy prior scale for each pairwise interaction is adjusted based on the range of response scores. Variables with more response categories have larger score products, so standardization ensures equivalent relative shrinkage across all pairs. Default: FALSE.





Sampler settings







Argument
Description




iter
Number of post-warmup iterations per chain. Default: 1000.


warmup
Number of warmup iterations before collecting samples. A minimum of 1000 is enforced. Default: 1000.


update_method
Sampling algorithm: "nuts" (No-U-Turn Sampler), "adaptive-metropolis" (componentwise Metropolis–Hastings with Robbins–Monro adaptation), or "hamiltonian-mc" (HMC with fixed path length). Default: "nuts".


target_accept
Target acceptance rate (0 to 1). Defaults: 0.44 for adaptive Metropolis, 0.65 for HMC, 0.80 for NUTS.


hmc_num_leapfrogs
Number of leapfrog steps for HMC. Default: 100.


nuts_max_depth
Maximum tree depth in NUTS. Default: 10.


learn_mass_matrix
Logical. If TRUE, adapt a diagonal mass matrix during warmup (HMC/NUTS only). Default: TRUE.


chains
Number of parallel chains. Default: 4.


cores
Number of CPU cores for parallel execution. Default: parallel::detectCores().


display_progress
Progress reporting: "per-chain", "total", or "none". Default: "per-chain".


seed
Optional integer seed for reproducibility.


pseudolikelihood
For mixed MRF models: "conditional" (conditions on continuous variables for discrete updates; faster) or "marginal" (integrates out continuous variables; more expensive). Ignored for pure ordinal or pure continuous data. Default: "conditional".


verbose
Logical. Print informational messages during data processing. Default: getOption("bgms.verbose", TRUE).

title: bgm()
text:
Value
A list of class "bgms" with posterior summaries, posterior mean matrices, and access to raw MCMC draws. The object can be passed to print(), summary(), and coef().
Main components:

posterior_summary_main — Data frame with posterior summaries (mean, sd, MCSE, ESS, Rhat) for main-effect parameters. For OMRF models these are category thresholds; for mixed MRF models these are discrete thresholds and continuous means. NULL for GGM models.
posterior_summary_quadratic — Data frame with posterior summaries for the precision matrix diagonal (GGM and mixed MRF). NULL for OMRF models.
posterior_summary_pairwise — Data frame with posterior summaries for pairwise interaction parameters.
posterior_summary_indicator — Data frame with posterior summaries for edge inclusion indicators (if edge_selection = TRUE).
posterior_mean_main — Posterior mean of main-effect parameters.
posterior_mean_pairwise — Symmetric matrix of posterior mean pairwise interaction strengths. For GGM and mixed MRF models, the precision matrix diagonal is on the matrix diagonal.
posterior_mean_indicator — Symmetric matrix of posterior mean inclusion probabilities (if edge selection was enabled).
raw_samples — A list of raw MCMC draws per chain, with sublists for main, pairwise, indicator, and allocations (SBM prior).
arguments — A list of function call arguments and metadata.

Additional summaries when edge_prior = "Stochastic-Block":

posterior_summary_pairwise_allocations — Data frame with posterior summaries for pairwise cluster co-occurrence.
posterior_coclustering_matrix — Symmetric co-clustering proportion matrix.
posterior_mean_allocations — Posterior mean cluster allocations.
posterior_mode_allocations — Posterior mode cluster allocations.
posterior_num_blocks — Posterior probabilities for each possible number of clusters.

NUTS diagnostics (tree depth, divergences, energy, E-BFMI) are available in fit$nuts_diag when update_method = "nuts".

title: bgm()
text:
Details

Ordinal variables
The function supports two types of ordinal variables.
Regular ordinal variables assign a category threshold parameter to each response category except the lowest. The model imposes no additional constraints on the distribution of category responses.
Blume–Capel ordinal variables assume a baseline category (e.g., a “neutral” response) and score responses by distance from this baseline. Category thresholds are modeled as:
\[\mu_c = \alpha \cdot (c - b) + \beta \cdot (c - b)^2\]
where \(\mu_c\) is the category threshold for category \(c\), \(\alpha\) is a linear trend across categories, \(\beta\) is a quadratic effect (negative values favor responses near the baseline; positive values favor extremes), and \(b\) is the baseline category.


Edge selection
When edge_selection = TRUE, the function performs Bayesian variable selection on pairwise interactions using spike-and-slab priors:

Bernoulli — Fixed inclusion probability across edges.
Beta-Bernoulli — Inclusion probability is given a Beta prior.
Stochastic-Block — Cluster-based edge priors with Beta, Dirichlet, and Poisson hyperpriors.



Prior distributions

Pairwise effects — Cauchy (slab) prior.
Main effects — Beta-prime distribution.
Edge indicators — Bernoulli, Beta-Bernoulli, or Stochastic-Block prior.



Sampling algorithms and warmup
Parameters are updated within a Gibbs framework using one of three algorithms:

Adaptive Metropolis–Hastings — Componentwise random-walk updates with Robbins–Monro proposal adaptation.
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo — Joint updates using fixed-length leapfrog trajectories. Step size is tuned during warmup via dual averaging; the diagonal mass matrix can also be adapted.
No-U-Turn Sampler — Adaptive extension of HMC with dynamically chosen trajectory lengths. Warmup uses a staged fast–slow–fast schedule.

When edge_selection = TRUE, edge-inclusion indicator updates are delayed until after the core warmup phase. The warmup schedule appends additional stages for proposal-SD tuning (Stage 3b) and graph initialization (Stage 3c), so the total warmup exceeds the user-specified value.


Missing data
If na_action = "listwise", rows with missing values are removed. If na_action = "impute", missing values are imputed within the MCMC loop via Gibbs sampling.

title: bgm()
text:
Examples

# Fit a model on a subset of the Wenchuan data
fit = bgm(x = Wenchuan[, 1:5], chains = 2)

# Posterior inclusion probabilities
summary(fit)$indicator

# Posterior pairwise effects
summary(fit)$pairwise

title: bgmCompare()
text:
Description
The bgmCompare function estimates group differences in category threshold parameters (main effects) and pairwise interactions (pairwise effects) of a Markov Random Field (MRF) for binary and ordinal variables. Groups can be defined either by supplying two separate datasets (x and y) or by a group membership vector. Optionally, Bayesian variable selection identifies differences across groups.

  y,
  group_indicator,
  difference_selection = TRUE,
  main_difference_selection = FALSE,
  variable_type = "ordinal",
  baseline_category,
  difference_scale = 1,
  difference_prior = c("Bernoulli", "Beta-Bernoulli"),
  difference_probability = 0.5,
  beta_bernoulli_alpha = 1,
  beta_bernoulli_beta = 1,
  pairwise_scale = 2.5,
  main_alpha = 0.5,
  main_beta = 0.5,

)

text:
Arguments

Data and groups







Argument
Description




x
A data frame or matrix of binary and ordinal responses for Group 1. Variables should be coded as nonnegative integers starting at 0. For ordinal variables, unused categories are collapsed; for Blume–Capel variables, all categories are retained.


y
Optional data frame or matrix for Group 2 (two-group designs). Must have the same variables (columns) as x.


group_indicator
Optional integer vector of group memberships for rows of x (multi-group designs). Ignored if y is supplied.


variable_type
Character vector specifying the type of each variable: "ordinal" (default) or "blume-capel".

Integer or vector giving the baseline category for Blume–Capel variables.

How to handle missing data: "listwise" (drop rows) or "impute" (impute within Gibbs). Default: "listwise".





Difference selection







Argument
Description




difference_selection
Logical. If TRUE, spike-and-slab priors are applied to difference parameters. Default: TRUE.


main_difference_selection
Logical. If TRUE, apply spike-and-slab selection to main effect (threshold) differences. Since main effects are often nuisance parameters and their selection can interfere with pairwise selection under the Beta-Bernoulli prior, the default is FALSE. Only used when difference_selection = TRUE.

standardize

Argument

Sampling algorithm: "nuts", "adaptive-metropolis", or "hamiltonian-mc". Default: "nuts".

text:
Value
A list of class "bgmCompare" containing posterior summaries, posterior mean matrices, and raw MCMC samples:

posterior_summary_main_baseline, posterior_summary_pairwise_baseline — Summaries of baseline thresholds and pairwise interactions.
posterior_summary_main_differences, posterior_summary_pairwise_differences — Summaries of group differences in thresholds and pairwise interactions.
posterior_summary_indicator — Summaries of inclusion indicators (if difference_selection = TRUE).
posterior_mean_main_baseline, posterior_mean_pairwise_baseline — Posterior mean matrices (legacy style).
raw_samples — List of raw draws per chain for main, pairwise, and indicator parameters.
arguments — List of function call arguments and metadata.

The summary() method prints formatted summaries, and coef() extracts posterior means. NUTS diagnostics are available in fit$nuts_diag when update_method = "nuts".

title: bgmCompare()
text:
Details

Pairwise interactions
For variables \(i\) and \(j\), the group-specific interaction is represented as:
\[\theta_{ij}^{(g)} = \phi_{ij} + \delta_{ij}^{(g)}\]
where \(\phi_{ij}\) is the baseline effect and \(\delta_{ij}^{(g)}\) are group differences constrained to sum to zero.


Ordinal variables
Regular ordinal variables: category thresholds are decomposed into a baseline plus group differences for each category.
Blume–Capel variables: category thresholds are quadratic in the category index, with both the linear and quadratic terms split into a baseline plus group differences.


Variable selection
When difference_selection = TRUE, spike-and-slab priors are applied to difference parameters:

Bernoulli — Fixed prior inclusion probability.
Beta-Bernoulli — Inclusion probability given a Beta prior.



Sampling algorithms and warmup
Parameters are updated within a Gibbs framework, using the same sampling algorithms and staged warmup scheme described in bgm(): adaptive Metropolis–Hastings, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, or the No-U-Turn Sampler. When difference_selection = TRUE, indicator updates are delayed until late warmup.

title: bgmCompare()
text:
Examples

# Compare French and non-French groups on a subset of the Boredom data
x = Boredom[Boredom$language == "fr", 2:6]
y = Boredom[Boredom$language != "fr", 2:6]

fit = bgmCompare(x, y, chains = 2)

# Posterior inclusion probabilities
summary(fit)$indicator

# Bayesian model averaged main effects for the groups

Every model must implement do_one_metropolis_step(). Models that support gradient-based samplers (NUTS, HMC) also override gradient() and logp_and_gradient(). The joint function is more efficient because the log-posterior and gradient share intermediate computations.

virtual void update_edge_indicators();

title: Model Classes
text:
GGMModel
Defined in src/models/ggm/ggm_model.h and ggm_model.cpp.
Parameterization. The GGM is parameterized by the precision matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) (inverse covariance). The model maintains an upper-triangular Cholesky factor \(\mathbf{R}\) such that \(\mathbf{R}^\top\mathbf{R} = \boldsymbol{\Omega}\).
Sampling. Because the precision matrix must remain positive definite, the GGM does not support gradient-based samplers. Instead, it uses element-wise Metropolis-Hastings: each off-diagonal element \(\omega_{ij}\) is proposed from a Gaussian centered on the current value. After each proposal, the Cholesky factor is updated via a rank-1 Givens rotation (or hyperbolic rotation for downdates), avoiding a full \(O(p^3)\) decomposition.
Sufficient statistics. For complete data, the GGM only needs the sufficient statistic \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\), not the raw data matrix. When missing data imputation is active, the sufficient statistics are recomputed after each imputation step.
Spike-and-slab. Edge indicators \(\gamma_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}\) control whether edge \((i,j)\) is included. When \(\gamma_{ij} = 0\), the corresponding precision element is fixed at zero.

title: Model Classes
text:
OMRFModel
Defined in src/models/omrf/omrf_model.h and omrf_model.cpp.
Parameterization. The ordinal MRF has two parameter types: main effects (category thresholds) and pairwise interactions. For ordinal variables, there is one threshold per category. For Blume-Capel variables, there are two parameters: a linear effect \(\alpha\) and a quadratic effect \(\beta\), with the category score \(\mu_c = \alpha(c - b) + \beta(c - b)^2\) where \(b\) is the reference category.
Gradient. The OMRF supports logp_and_gradient(), enabling NUTS and HMC sampling. The gradient involves category probabilities computed by the variable helpers, which use a FAST/SAFE dual-path strategy for numerical stability.
Residual matrix. The model maintains a precomputed residual matrix \(\mathbf{R}_{ni} = \sum_{j \neq i} x_{nj} \sigma_{ij}\) that caches the contribution of pairwise interactions to each variable’s conditional distribution. This matrix is updated incrementally when a single interaction changes.
Metropolis fallback. Even when NUTS is the primary sampler, the OMRF uses element-wise Metropolis proposals for edge indicator updates during the edge selection phase.

title: Model Classes
text:
MixedMRFModel
Defined in src/models/mixed/mixed_mrf_model.h and four .cpp files.
Parameterization. The mixed MRF handles \(p\) discrete and \(q\) continuous variables jointly. The log-density has the form:
\[
\log f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \sum_i \mu_i(x_i) + \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{K}_{xx} \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{K}_{yy} \mathbf{y} + 2\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{K}_{xy} \mathbf{y}
\]
where \(\mathbf{K}_{xx}\), \(\mathbf{K}_{yy}\), and \(\mathbf{K}_{xy}\) are the discrete-discrete, continuous-continuous, and cross-type interaction matrices.
Hybrid sampling. The NUTS block updates thresholds, discrete pairwise interactions (\(\mathbf{K}_{xx}\)), continuous means, and cross-type interactions (\(\mathbf{K}_{xy}\)). The continuous precision elements (\(\mathbf{K}_{yy}\)) are excluded from the NUTS block because the precision matrix must remain positive definite; they are updated by a separate element-wise Metropolis step (do_pairwise_continuous_metropolis_step()), analogous to the GGM.
Three dimension concepts. The model distinguishes:

parameter_dimension() — Active NUTS parameters (excludes inactive edges and \(\mathbf{K}_{yy}\))
full_parameter_dimension() — All NUTS-block parameters (includes inactive edges, excludes \(\mathbf{K}_{yy}\))
storage_dimension() — All parameters including \(\mathbf{K}_{yy}\) (what gets saved to output)

Pseudolikelihood options. The pseudolikelihood argument controls whether the model uses conditional or marginal pseudolikelihood for the continuous block. See the User’s Guide for the statistical distinction.

title: OMRF Internals
text:
Warning

Implementation details of the ordinal Markov random field in bgms. Source: src/models/omrf/omrf_model.h and omrf_model.cpp.

title: OMRF Internals
text:
Ordinal threshold parameterization
For an ordinal variable \(X_i\) with \(K_i\) categories \((0, 1, \ldots, K_i - 1)\), the model assigns one threshold parameter \(\mu_i(c)\) per category \(c\). The category \(c = 0\) serves as the reference with \(\mu_i(0) = 0\). The conditional probability of observing category \(c\) for person \(n\) is:
\[
P(X_{ni} = c \mid \text{rest}) = \frac{\exp\!\bigl(\mu_i(c) + c \cdot r_{ni}\bigr)}{\sum_{k=0}^{K_i - 1} \exp\!\bigl(\mu_i(k) + k \cdot r_{ni}\bigr)}
\]
where \(r_{ni} = \sum_{j \neq i} x_{nj}\, \sigma_{ij}\) is the residual score summarizing the pairwise interactions with all other variables.

title: OMRF Internals
text:
Blume-Capel model
For Blume-Capel variables, the threshold structure is replaced by two parameters: a linear effect \(\alpha_i\) and a quadratic effect \(\beta_i\). The category score is:
\[
\mu_i(c) = \alpha_i (c - b_i) + \beta_i (c - b_i)^2
\]
where \(b_i\) is the reference (baseline) category. This allows the model to capture non-monotone category effects, such as preferences for moderate responses.

title: OMRF Internals
text:
Residual matrix
The model maintains a precomputed \(n \times p\) residual matrix where entry \((n, i)\) stores:
\[
r_{ni} = \sum_{j \neq i} x_{nj}\, \sigma_{ij}
\]
When a single interaction \(\sigma_{ij}\) changes by \(\delta\), the residual matrix is updated incrementally:

Column \(i\): \(r_{ni} \leftarrow r_{ni} + \delta \cdot x_{nj}\) for all \(n\)
Column \(j\): \(r_{nj} \leftarrow r_{nj} + \delta \cdot x_{ni}\) for all \(n\)

This avoids recomputing the full matrix product after each parameter update.

title: OMRF Internals
text:
Pseudolikelihood
The OMRF uses a pseudolikelihood approximation: the product of full conditional distributions rather than the intractable joint distribution. The log-pseudolikelihood is:
\[
\text{PL}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \sum_{i=1}^{p} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \log P(X_{ni} = x_{ni} \mid \text{rest})
\]
The gradient of the log-pseudolikelihood with respect to each parameter involves the expected category values under the current conditionals, computed by the variable helpers.

title: OMRF Internals
text:
Gradient computation
The logp_and_gradient() method computes both the log-pseudoposterior and its gradient in a single pass. The gradient for a pairwise interaction \(\sigma_{ij}\) accumulates over all persons:
\[
\frac{\partial \text{PL}}{\partial \sigma_{ij}} = \sum_{n=1}^{N} \bigl(x_{ni} - E[X_i \mid \text{rest}]\bigr)\, x_{nj} + \bigl(x_{nj} - E[X_j \mid \text{rest}]\bigr)\, x_{ni}
\]
The expected values \(E[X_i \mid \text{rest}]\) are computed from the category probabilities, which are obtained via the numerically stable FAST/SAFE paths in variable_helpers.cpp.

title: OMRF Internals
text:
Edge indicator updates
When edge selection is active, the model performs a full scan over all \(p(p-1)/2\) edges after each gradient-based step. For each edge \((i, j)\):

Compute the pseudolikelihood ratio for inclusion vs. exclusion
Combine with the prior inclusion probability to get the posterior inclusion probability
Sample the indicator \(\gamma_{ij} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_{ij})\)
If the indicator changes, update the residual matrix accordingly

The scan order is randomized at each iteration via prepare_iteration(), which calls arma_randperm().

title: OMRF Internals
text:
Adaptive Metropolis fallback
Even when NUTS is the primary sampler, the OMRF implements element-wise adaptive Metropolis proposals for use during warmup stage 3b (proposal SD learning) and as a user-selectable alternative via interaction_scale = "fixed". The proposal SDs are tuned by Robbins-Monro targeting 0.234 acceptance, clamped to \([0.001, 2.0]\).

title: Variable Helpers
text:
Warning

Numerically stable computation of MRF category denominators and probabilities. Source: src/utils/variable_helpers.h and variable_helpers.cpp.

title: Variable Helpers
text:
The problem
MRF conditional probabilities involve exponentials of residual scores. For large networks or extreme parameter values, the arguments to exp() can exceed the IEEE 754 double-precision range, producing Inf or underflowing to zero. Naive computation (direct exponentiation followed by normalization) fails silently in these cases.

title: Variable Helpers
text:
The FAST/SAFE dual-path strategy
Every denominator and probability function in variable_helpers.cpp uses a two-path approach:

FAST path — Precomputed exponentials with power-chain accumulation. Used when the exponent arguments stay within safe bounds.
SAFE path — Direct log-sum-exp evaluation as a fallback when bounds are violated.

The choice is made per-person (per row of the data matrix) based on whether the residual score times the maximum category exceeds the EXP_BOUND threshold.

FAST path detail
For an ordinal variable with categories \(0, 1, \ldots, K-1\) and residual \(r\):

Precompute \(e_r = \exp(r)\) and \(e_m = \exp(\mu(c))\) for each category
Accumulate the denominator as a Horner-like chain: \(D = e^{-b}(1 + e_m[1] \cdot e_r + e_m[2] \cdot e_r^2 + \cdots)\) where \(b\) is a stabilizing shift

This avoids computing exp() for each category-residual combination independently and exploits the geometric structure of the category scores.


SAFE path detail
When the FAST path would overflow or underflow:

Compute \(s_c = \mu(c) + c \cdot r\) for each category
Find \(s_{\max} = \max_c s_c\)
Compute \(D = \exp(s_{\max}) \sum_c \exp(s_c - s_{\max})\)

This is the standard log-sum-exp trick, applied per person.


Block scanning
The functions process persons in contiguous blocks. Within each block, all persons follow the same path (FAST or SAFE). The block boundaries are determined by scanning the residual vector for bound violations. This enables branch-free vectorization within each block.

title: Variable Helpers
text:
Ordinal variables

compute_denom_ordinal()
Computes the normalization constant (denominator) for each person’s conditional distribution. Takes the residual vector, main-effect vector, and precomputed bound vector. Returns a vector of length \(n\).


compute_probs_ordinal()
Computes the full category probability matrix (\(n \times K\)) for one ordinal variable. Probabilities are clamped at zero to prevent negative values from floating-point error in the normalization step.

title: Variable Helpers
text:
Blume-Capel variables

compute_denom_blume_capel()
Handles the Blume-Capel parameterization, where the category score involves both linear and quadratic terms: \(\mu(c) = \alpha(c - b) + \beta(c - b)^2\). The precomputation of \(\theta_c = \alpha(c - b) + \beta(c - b)^2\) is done once per variable, and the FAST/SAFE split proceeds as for ordinal variables.


compute_probs_blume_capel()
Analogous to the ordinal version, but with the Blume-Capel category scores.

title: Variable Helpers
text:
Joint log-normalizer and probabilities
The LogZAndProbs struct bundles the log-normalizer \(\log Z\) and the probability matrix into a single return value. The joint computation functions (compute_logZ_and_probs_ordinal(), compute_logZ_and_probs_blume_capel()) share work between the two quantities, avoiding redundant exponential evaluations.
These joint functions are used in the gradient computation, where both the log-pseudolikelihood (which needs \(\log Z\)) and the gradient (which needs category probabilities) are computed in the same pass.

title: Variable Helpers
text:
The EXP_BOUND = 709 threshold
The bound that triggers the SAFE path is set to 709, derived from IEEE 754 double precision: \(\exp(709) \approx 8.2 \times 10^{307}\) is the largest representable value, while \(\exp(710) = \text{Inf}\). The FAST path checks whether \(|r| \cdot (K - 1) < 709\) before proceeding.

title: Mixed MRF Internals
text:
Block structure
The mixed MRF handles \(p\) discrete and \(q\) continuous variables. The parameter space is organized into three interaction blocks plus main effects:









Block
Parameters
Size
Sampler




Main effects
Discrete thresholds + continuous means
\(\text{thresholds} + q\)

\(p(p-1)/2\)

The continuous precision \(\mathbf{K}_{yy}\) must remain positive definite, so it is excluded from the NUTS block and updated by element-wise Metropolis proposals with Cholesky rank-1 updates, identical to the GGM strategy.

title: Mixed MRF Internals
text:
Parameter vector layout
The model distinguishes three vector types:

Active vector (parameter_dimension())
Contains only the parameters that NUTS updates, excluding edges set to zero by edge selection:
[ thresholds | K_xx (active) | means | K_xy (active) ]
The mass matrix and gradient are dimensioned to this vector.


Full vector (full_parameter_dimension())
Contains all NUTS-block parameters including inactive edges:
[ thresholds | K_xx (all) | means | K_xy (all) ]
Used for storage and initialization.


Storage vector (storage_dimension())
Adds the Metropolis-updated continuous precision to the full vector:
[ thresholds | K_xx (all) | means | K_xy (all) | K_yy (all) ]
This is what gets saved to ChainResult::samples at each iteration.

title: Mixed MRF Internals
text:
Hybrid sampling strategy
Each MCMC iteration has two phases:

NUTS phase — Update the active parameter vector (thresholds, \(\mathbf{K}_{xx}\), means, \(\mathbf{K}_{xy}\)) using one NUTS step. The logp_and_gradient() method computes the log-pseudoposterior and gradient for this block only.
Metropolis phase — Update the continuous precision elements (\(\mathbf{K}_{yy}\)) one at a time via do_pairwise_continuous_metropolis_step(). Each proposal uses a Gaussian perturbation with Robbins-Monro-tuned SD, followed by a Cholesky rank-1 update to maintain positive definiteness.

Edge indicator updates (when active) operate on all three interaction blocks.

title: Mixed MRF Internals
text:
Gradient computation
The gradient (mixed_mrf_gradient.cpp) is computed for the NUTS block only. It involves:

Discrete conditionals — Category probabilities via variable helpers, contributing gradients for thresholds and \(\mathbf{K}_{xx}\)
Cross-type terms — Contributions from \(\mathbf{K}_{xy}\) to both discrete and continuous conditional distributions
Continuous means — Gradient of the continuous-variable contribution to the pseudolikelihood

The log-prior gradient adds the Cauchy prior penalty on pairwise interactions.

title: Mixed MRF Internals
text:
Pseudolikelihood options
The pseudolikelihood argument controls the continuous-variable likelihood:

"conditional" (default) — Uses the conditional distribution of each continuous variable given the rest, consistent with the discrete pseudolikelihood
"marginal" — Uses the marginal normal likelihood for the continuous block, which can be more efficient when \(q\) is large

The choice affects both the log-posterior evaluation and the gradient computation.

title: Mixed MRF Internals
text:
Missing data
The mixed MRF tracks missing indices separately for discrete and continuous variables (missing_index_discrete, missing_index_continuous). During imputation:

Missing discrete values are sampled from their full conditional categorical distributions
Missing continuous values are sampled from their conditional normal distributions given the current precision matrix

title: Mixed MRF Internals
text:
Output assembly
The R output builder (build_output_mixed_mrf() in build_output.R) maps the flat storage vector back to the original variable ordering using fill_mixed_symmetric(). This function places discrete-discrete, continuous-continuous, and cross-type interactions into the correct cells of the \((p+q) \times (p+q)\) output matrix, respecting the original column order (which may interleave discrete and continuous variables).

title: Edge Priors

The edge prior framework controls which edges are included in the graph. All priors inherit from BaseEdgePrior in src/priors/edge_prior.h.

title: Edge Priors
Edge Priors
text:
BernoulliEdgePrior
The simplest prior: each edge has a fixed inclusion probability that does not change during sampling. The update() method is a no-op.
This prior is used when the user specifies edge_prior = "Bernoulli" with a fixed inclusion probability matrix.

title: Edge Priors
text:
BetaBernoulliEdgePrior
A conjugate prior that learns a shared inclusion probability from the data. At each iteration:

Count the number of included edges: \(k = \sum_{i<j} \gamma_{ij}\)
Count the total number of possible edges: \(m = p(p-1)/2\)
Draw a new inclusion probability: \(\pi \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha + k,\; \beta + m - k)\)
Set all entries of the inclusion probability matrix to \(\pi\)

The hyperparameters \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) default to 1 (uniform prior on the inclusion probability).
This is the default edge prior in bgms (edge_prior = "Beta-Bernoulli").

title: Edge Priors
text:
StochasticBlockEdgePrior
The stochastic block model (SBM) prior assigns variables to latent clusters and allows different inclusion probabilities for within-cluster and between-cluster edges. See SBM Prior for the full formulation.
The StochasticBlockEdgePrior class stores:

cluster_allocations_ — Current cluster assignment for each variable
cluster_prob_ — \(K \times K\) matrix of block inclusion probabilities
log_Vn_ — Log partition coefficients for the MFM prior on cluster count

Its update() method runs collapsed Gibbs sampling to update cluster assignments and block probabilities (delegated to functions in sbm_edge_prior.cpp).
has_allocations() returns true, and get_allocations() returns the current cluster assignment vector. These are stored in ChainResult::allocation_samples for post-hoc analysis.

The R layer sits between user-facing functions (bgm(), bgmCompare()) and the C++ engine. It validates inputs, constructs a specification object, dispatches to the appropriate C++ sampler, and assembles the returned output into an S3 fit object.

text:
Data flow

  ↓
bgm_spec()            ← validates, assembles sub-lists
  ↓

Both bgm() and bgmCompare() follow this pipeline. The bgmCompare() path adds group-specific preprocessing (projection matrices, group indices, precomputed sufficient statistics) before the spec is constructed.

title: R Scaffolding
text:
Validation pipeline
Validation is split across four files, each with a focused scope.

Data checks (validate_data.R)
data_check() is the entry point. It enforces:

Input is a data frame or matrix (converts to integer matrix for ordinal data)
No constant columns
At least two variables
Column names exist and are unique
For ordinal data: all values are non-negative integers

Missing data handling branches on na_action:

"listwise" — rows with any NA are dropped
"impute" — missing indices are recorded for Bayesian imputation in C++



Variable type detection (validate_model.R)
validate_variable_types() classifies each column as "ordinal" or "blume-capel" (for discrete variables) based on the variable_type argument. When variable_type = "ordinal" (the default), all discrete variables are treated as ordinal. When a named vector is provided, each variable is classified individually.
validate_baseline_category() sets the reference category for Blume-Capel variables. The default (0) places the reference at the lowest observed category.


Sampler validation (validate_sampler.R)
validate_sampler() resolves the interaction_scale argument into a concrete sampler type ("nuts", "hmc", or "adaptive_metropolis") and sets defaults for tuning parameters (target_accept, nuts_max_depth, hmc_num_leapfrogs). It detects the number of available cores and resolves the progress display type.


Edge prior validation (validate_model.R)
validate_edge_prior() and validate_difference_prior() map string names ("Bernoulli", "Beta-Bernoulli", "Stochastic-Block") to validated prior configurations. For the SBM prior, the six hyperparameters (beta_bernoulli_alpha, beta_bernoulli_beta, beta_bernoulli_alpha_between, beta_bernoulli_beta_between, dirichlet_alpha, lambda) are checked and defaults applied.

Output assembly (build_output.R)
build_output() transforms raw C++ output into the S3 objects returned to the user ("bgms" or "bgmCompare" class).

GGM and OMRF (build_output_bgm())
The GGM and OMRF paths share a unified builder. Key operations:

Normalize raw samples — Split the flat parameter vector into main-effect and pairwise-interaction matrices per chain
Compute posterior means — Average across iterations and chains
Compute inclusion probabilities — Average indicator samples (when edge selection is active)
Assemble $raw_samples — Per-chain lists of main, pairwise, indicator, and allocations matrices
NUTS diagnostics — When available, collect tree depth, divergence, and energy samples into $nuts_diagnostics
Warmup check — Collect $warmup_check from C++



Mixed MRF (build_output_mixed_mrf())
The mixed MRF builder handles the block structure: discrete-discrete, continuous-continuous, and cross-type interactions are stored in separate blocks by C++ and need to be mapped back to the original variable ordering.


Compare (build_output_compare())
The comparison builder splits posterior means into group-level ($group_posterior_means) and difference ($difference_posterior_means) components, and computes difference inclusion probabilities.

bgms uses a multi-stage warmup schedule to tune MCMC sampler parameters before collecting posterior samples. The schedule is defined in src/mcmc/execution/warmup_schedule.h and adapts its structure based on whether edge selection is active.

title: Warmup Schedule
text:
Five stages
The warmup period is divided into five stages. Stages 3b and 3c only apply when edge selection is enabled.








Stage
Name
Purpose




1
Initial exploration
Find a reasonable region of parameter space


2
Adaptation windows
Tune step size (dual averaging) and mass matrix (Welford)


3a
Terminal window
Final mass matrix and step-size adaptation


3b
Proposal SD learning
Tune element-wise Metropolis proposal SDs with edge selection active


3c
Step-size re-adaptation
Re-adapt the NUTS/HMC step size after edge selection changes the geometry




Stage 1: Initial exploration
A short burn-in phase (default: the first 75 iterations). The sampler explores freely; no mass matrix accumulation occurs. Dual averaging runs to coarsely tune the step size.


Stage 2: Adaptation windows
The step size and mass matrix are tuned in expanding windows. The first window has 25 iterations. Each subsequent window doubles in size (25 → 50 → 100 → …) until the stage 3a boundary is reached. At the end of each window:

The accumulated variance from DiagMassMatrixAccumulator is extracted as the new diagonal mass matrix
The step-size heuristic runs again with the new mass matrix
Both accumulators are reset for the next window



Stage 3a: Terminal window
The last adaptation window before edge selection activates. After this stage, the mass matrix is frozen.


Stage 3b: Proposal SD learning
When edge selection is active, the model needs element-wise Metropolis proposal standard deviations for the edge indicator updates. During stage 3b, edge selection is turned on and the proposal SDs are tuned via Robbins-Monro updates:
\[
\sigma_{k+1} = \sigma_k \cdot \exp\!\bigl(w_k (\log \alpha_k - \log \alpha^*)\bigr)
\]
where \(\alpha_k\) is the observed acceptance probability and \(\alpha^*\) is the target (default 0.234). The updated SD is clamped to \([0.001, 2.0]\).


Stage 3c: Step-size re-adaptation
After edge selection changes the effective posterior geometry (many edges may be set to zero), the NUTS/HMC step size needs readjustment. Stage 3c runs dual averaging one more time with the final mass matrix and active edge selection.

title: Warmup Schedule
text:
Budget allocation
When edge selection is active, the total warmup budget is split as:

Stages 1–3a: 85% of total warmup
Stage 3b: 10% (skipped if fewer than 20 iterations)
Stage 3c: ~5%

When edge selection is inactive, stages 3b and 3c are skipped and the full budget is allocated to stages 1–3a.

title: Warmup Schedule
text:
Warning system
The WarmupSchedule tracks a warning_type field that records when the warmup budget is insufficient:



Code
Meaning




0
No warning


1
Warmup too short for the standard schedule


2
Proportional fallback used (reduced window sizes)


3
Limited tuning (fewer adaptation windows)


4
Proposal SD learning skipped (stage 3b dropped)



The warmup_check table returned by bgm() reports these warnings per chain, accessible via fit$warmup_check in R.

An end-to-end analysis of binary data using the ordinal Markov random field. This example uses the ADHD dataset bundled with bgms.

title: Binary Network
text:
Data
The ADHD dataset contains binary symptom ratings for 355 children. The first column is a group indicator (ADHD diagnosis); columns 2–19 are nine Inattentive and nine Hyperactive/Impulsive items scored as present (1) or absent (0). We drop the group column and analyze the first five Inattentive items.

library(bgms)
data = ADHD[, 2:6]
head(data)

title: Binary Network
text:
Fit the model
Binary variables are a special case of ordinal data (two categories). bgm() fits an ordinal MRF with spike-and-slab edge selection by default.

fit = bgm(data, seed = 1234)

title: Binary Network
text:
Posterior summaries

summary(fit)
coef(fit)

title: Binary Network
text:
Edge selection
The posterior inclusion probabilities indicate the evidence for each edge:

coef(fit)$indicator

Convert to Bayes factors when the prior inclusion probability equals 0.5:

p = coef(fit)$indicator[1, 2]
BF_10 = p / (1 - p)       # evidence for inclusion
1 / BF_10                  # evidence for exclusion

title: Binary Network
text:
Interpretation
Threshold the inclusion probabilities at 0.5 and plot.

library(qgraph)

median_probability_network = coef(fit)$pairwise
median_probability_network[coef(fit)$indicator < 0.5] = 0.0

qgraph(median_probability_network,
  theme = "TeamFortress",
  maximum = 1,
  fade = FALSE,
  color = c("#f0ae0e"), vsize = 10, repulsion = .9,
  label.cex = 1, label.scale = "FALSE",
  labels = colnames(data)
)
